AI Consultancy Data strategy. AI strategy. New operating models. One team. Most brands have the ambition but not the architecture. We help you build the data foundations, deploy AI where it moves the business, automate what should not be manual, and restructure the team to run it as a capability rather than a one-off project. Discuss your strategy → How we work 92% Plan AI improvements ConvertMate, 2026 40.6% Actually doing it ConvertMate, 2026 51.4% Execution gap ConvertMate, 2026 3 Maturity stages Inflexion model 01. The gap The ambition is there. The architecture isn't. 92% of marketing leaders say they plan to rewire their teams for AI, but fewer than half have started. The gap is not willingness. It is knowing what to do, in what order, and how to make it stick. The problem is structural. Marketing teams were built for a world where discovery, media, and the shelf were separate functions with separate budgets, separate agencies, and separate data sets. AI reads them all as one signal. The operating model has not caught up. We help close that gap. Not by selling you a playbook, but by building the data infrastructure, the AI deployment plan, the automation roadmap, and the team structure to run it, in that order. 02. What we do Four capabilities that feed each other. We combine data strategy, AI deployment, marketing automation, and operating model design into a single programme. Each feeds the next. I. Data strategy Connect the data that connects the channels. Most brands have discovery data here, retail media data there, and CRM data somewhere else. We build the unified data layer that lets you see the full picture and measure what moves the business. II. AI strategy Deploy AI where it moves the business. We assess where AI can improve output, including citation work, content generation, media allocation and customer insight, then build the deployment plan that matches your maturity level. III. Marketing automation Automate what shouldn't be manual. Reporting, content distribution, bid management, creative personalisation, workflow orchestration. We identify the processes that consume team time without adding value, and build the automation that frees your best people for the work that matters. IV. Operating model Restructure the team to run it. The technology is the easy part. The hard part is reorganising the team around the new model. We design the structure, roles, processes and governance needed to run the new operating model without relying on the people who built it. 03. Maturity model Three stages. Most teams are in stage one. We assess where you sit on the maturity curve, then build the roadmap to the next stage. The goal is not to leap to stage three overnight. It is to make consistent progress that compounds. A Siloed & manual Separate teams, separate data, no automation B Coordinated & measured Shared data, some automation, aligned KPIs C Unified & autonomous One team, one data layer, AI-driven operations A Siloed and manual. Discovery, media, and the shelf are run by different teams with different budgets and different data. Reporting is manual. Decisions are made on lagging indicators. Automation is limited to basic bid management. Most brands are here. B Coordinated and measured. Data is shared across functions. Common KPIs exist. Automation handles routine reporting and optimisation. The team is beginning to connect discovery and shelf signals. AI is used for content generation and basic analysis. C Unified and autonomous. One team runs discovery and the shelf with a single data layer. AI drives content creation, media allocation, citation work, and personalisation. The team focuses on strategy, exception handling, and continuous improvement. The operating model is sustainable. 04. The maturity model, applied Where most teams sit, and where they go next. The A-to-C maturity spectrum is not a theoretical model. It is based on patterns we see across brands that have attempted AI restructuring. Most brands are at A: siloed teams, manual processes, separate data sets. A minority reach B, where shared data and some automation exist. Almost none are at C. The roadmap from A to B takes 12 to 16 weeks in our experience. The roadmap from B to C requires a full operating-model redesign and board-level commitment. We tell you where you sit and what it takes to move to the next stage. Discuss your strategy → 05. The first quarter From assessment to a team that can run it. 01 Weeks 1–3: baseline Maturity assessment, data infrastructure audit, stakeholder alignment. You see where you sit on the A–C spectrum and what needs to change first. 02 Weeks 4–6: design Operating model designed, technology roadmap agreed, measurement framework built. Specified to role and responsibility level. 03 Weeks 7–12: build Data infrastructure deployed, automation workflows built, first AI use cases in production. Team training completed. 04 Ongoing: advise Board-level advisory as the landscape shifts. The team runs it; we provide assurance, course correction, and continuous improvement. 06. Why this matters now The team structure that worked in 2020 is already obsolete. 01 Execution is no longer the bottleneck. AI tools handle content creation, bid management, reporting and creative personalisation. The bottleneck is now strategic: what to prioritise, how to interpret the data, and when human judgement must override the machine. 02 Separate teams for discovery, media and the shelf hide the compounding effects. AI reads discovery signals, retail media signals and Amazon signals as one picture. The team structure should reflect that. Most brands still organise around channels that no longer exist as separate consumer experiences. 03 The operating model determines what is possible. The best AI deployment plan fails if the team cannot execute it. We design the structure, roles and governance first, then select the technology. Technology without operating-model change is the most expensive way to stay where you are. You know what needs to change. We can show you how. A structured maturity assessment and a roadmap to the next stage. You keep the output either way. Discuss your strategy → AI consultancy that ships operating models. retail-media.title: Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf | Inflexion
retail-media.body_text: Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf The shelf is now an algorithm. Position is determined by signals, not by spend. Retail media is the fastest-growing channel in marketing, and it is often misunderstood. We separate paid and organic position, distinguish useful signals from noise, and report share of shelf separately from blended ROAS. Audit your shelf position → How the algorithm works $300B Retail media spend (2026) Source: GroupM, eMarketer 60% Amazon share of retail media Source: eMarketer, 2026 15.9% AI referral conversion rate Source: Seer Interactive, 2025 4.4× Organic vs paid ROAS Source: Marketplace Pulse, 2025 The real mechanics What the algorithm rewards, and what most retail media setups get wrong. The retail-media algorithm determines position from a weighted set of signals. No retailer publishes the full formula, but the inputs are known from published documentation and empirical testing: relevance (how well the product matches the search term), conversion rate (how often the page converts), click-through rate (how often the listing earns a click when shown), price competitiveness (relative to alternatives shown on the same page), review velocity and sentiment (recency and quality of customer reviews), and inventory depth (availability and delivery speed). The most common mistake is treating retail media as a pure media buy: set a budget, bid on terms, adjust bids. That approach works only when the non-media signals are already competitive. If conversion rate, reviews or product data are weak, additional spend buys more of the same position. The constraint is seldom the bid. We separate paid position from organic position in our reporting. A share-of-shelf number that hides how much was bought does not measure performance; it reports media spend. 71% Of Amazon units from organic Source: Jungle Scout, 2025 3× Better organic = lower CPC Source: Profitero, 2025 82% Shoppers ignore sponsored-only Source: Nielsen, 2025 2.1M Amazon sellers (2026) Source: Marketplace Pulse The platforms Where we work and how. Each platform has its own signal weighting and ad product structure. A strategy that works on Amazon does not transfer directly to Instacart, and neither works the same as Walmart Connect. We tailor the approach per platform and report them separately. Amazon Sponsored Products, Brands, Display and DSP. Run as one campaign system, not four separate products. Amazon rewards product data completeness, conversion history and inventory depth alongside bid. We improve all four, not just the bid. Walmart Walmart Connect. Different signal weighting: Walmart places heavier emphasis on omnichannel sales data and in-store availability. The ad products are less mature but growing fast. Early adoption may provide an advantage, but the effect should be measured. Instacart CPG-focused retail media. Heavily weighted toward category relevance and promotional history. Shelf position on Instacart behaves differently from Amazon because the buying intent is different: immediate delivery rather than catalogue browsing. Off-platform Criteo, The Trade Desk, retail data partnerships. Off-platform paid and social activity drives traffic into the retail algorithm. We plan this alongside the retail media, not separately, because the traffic quality entering the funnel affects the algorithm's read of your product. The audit What we actually check. A full retail media audit looks beyond the bid. These are the signals we check on each engagement. 01 Product data completeness. Titles, bullet points, images, A+ content, attributes, backend search terms. The algorithm reads this before it reads the bid. Incomplete product data is the most common constraint we find. 02 Review velocity and sentiment. How quickly reviews accumulate and what they say. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. A product with 500 old reviews can be outperformed by a product with 50 recent positive ones. 03 Conversion rate by traffic source. We track organic, sponsored and external conversion separately. A blended number hides whether the problem is product or placement. 04 Price and promotion competitiveness. Relative to the alternatives shown on the same search results page and product detail page. We benchmark pricing, coupon depth and deal timing against category competitors. 05 Inventory depth and fulfilment. Stock-outs, shipping speed and fulfilment method all feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is improved. 06 Paid position vs organic position. We separate the two in every report. If position improves but conversion does not follow, we flag it rather than present it as success. The approach Map the signals, then allocate the budget. The starting point on every engagement is a full shelf baseline: paid and organic positions separated, product signals audited, competitive landscape documented. The baseline determines the order of work. In most cases, product data fixes come first, review velocity improvements second, and media allocation third. The bid is rarely the constraint. We report rank and conversion separately so you can see which is improving and which is not. We tell you before you commit budget if a category's top position is defended by spend levels that make chasing it a negative-ROI decision. The algorithm changes without notice, and we adjust before the data shows a problem. The first quarter From standing start to a restructured programme. 01 Weeks 1–3: baseline Shelf position mapped, paid and organic separated. Signal audit completed. Category competitive landscape documented. 02 Weeks 4–6: plan One plan across retail media and the paid/social spend feeding it. Product data improvements identified. Measurement agreed. 03 Weeks 7–12: build Campaign structures rebuilt. Product data improved. Creative produced. Shipped by the same team that did the diagnostic. 04 Ongoing: track Weekly bid and budget improvement against share of shelf. Monthly strategy review with full reporting. What you get Concrete deliverables. Every engagement produces the same set of outputs. You keep the baseline whether you continue or not. 01 A shelf position baseline you keep. Paid and organic positions, separated. Category competitive landscape. Signal audit. Whether or not you continue. 02 A written plan with prioritisation reasoning shown. Not a list of campaign ideas. Why each item, in what order, and what it is expected to move. 03 A weekly tracked report against the baseline. Share of shelf, split paid and organic, tracked against conversion. Changes signalled, not buried. 04 One team, not an account layer. The people who ran the audit are the people who manage the campaigns. No handoffs, no dropped context. Your shelf position is measurable. Find out where you stand. We run a full audit across Amazon, Walmart and Instacart. You keep the baseline either way. sections.heading: What the algorithm rewards,and what most retail media setups get wrong.
sections.text: The real mechanics What the algorithm rewards, and what most retail media setups get wrong. The retail-media algorithm determines position from a weighted set of signals. No retailer publishes the full formula, but the inputs are known from published documentation and empirical testing: relevance (how well the product matches the search term), conversion rate (how often the page converts), click-through rate (how often the listing earns a click when shown), price competitiveness (relative to alternatives shown on the same page), review velocity and sentiment (recency and quality of customer reviews), and inventory depth (availability and delivery speed). The most common mistake is treating retail media as a pure media buy: set a budget, bid on terms, adjust bids. That approach works only when the non-media signals are already competitive. If conversion rate, reviews or product data are weak, additional spend buys more of the same position. The constraint is seldom the bid. We separate paid position from organic position in our reporting. A share-of-shelf number that hides how much was bought does not measure performance; it reports media spend. 71% Of Amazon units from organic Source: Jungle Scout, 2025 3× Better organic = lower CPC Source: Profitero, 2025 82% Shoppers ignore sponsored-only Source: Nielsen, 2025 2.1M Amazon sellers (2026) Source: Marketplace Pulse

sections.heading: Where we workand how.
sections.text: The platforms Where we work and how. Each platform has its own signal weighting and ad product structure. A strategy that works on Amazon does not transfer directly to Instacart, and neither works the same as Walmart Connect. We tailor the approach per platform and report them separately. Amazon Sponsored Products, Brands, Display and DSP. Run as one campaign system, not four separate products. Amazon rewards product data completeness, conversion history and inventory depth alongside bid. We improve all four, not just the bid. Walmart Walmart Connect. Different signal weighting: Walmart places heavier emphasis on omnichannel sales data and in-store availability. The ad products are less mature but growing fast. Early adoption may provide an advantage, but the effect should be measured. Instacart CPG-focused retail media. Heavily weighted toward category relevance and promotional history. Shelf position on Instacart behaves differently from Amazon because the buying intent is different: immediate delivery rather than catalogue browsing. Off-platform Criteo, The Trade Desk, retail data partnerships. Off-platform paid and social activity drives traffic into the retail algorithm. We plan this alongside the retail media, not separately, because the traffic quality entering the funnel affects the algorithm's read of your product.

sections.heading: What we actuallycheck.
sections.text: The audit What we actually check. A full retail media audit looks beyond the bid. These are the signals we check on each engagement. 01 Product data completeness. Titles, bullet points, images, A+ content, attributes, backend search terms. The algorithm reads this before it reads the bid. Incomplete product data is the most common constraint we find. 02 Review velocity and sentiment. How quickly reviews accumulate and what they say. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. A product with 500 old reviews can be outperformed by a product with 50 recent positive ones. 03 Conversion rate by traffic source. We track organic, sponsored and external conversion separately. A blended number hides whether the problem is product or placement. 04 Price and promotion competitiveness. Relative to the alternatives shown on the same search results page and product detail page. We benchmark pricing, coupon depth and deal timing against category competitors. 05 Inventory depth and fulfilment. Stock-outs, shipping speed and fulfilment method all feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is improved. 06 Paid position vs organic position. We separate the two in every report. If position improves but conversion does not follow, we flag it rather than present it as success.

sections.heading: Map the signals, then allocate the budget.
sections.text: The approach Map the signals, then allocate the budget. The starting point on every engagement is a full shelf baseline: paid and organic positions separated, product signals audited, competitive landscape documented. The baseline determines the order of work. In most cases, product data fixes come first, review velocity improvements second, and media allocation third. The bid is rarely the constraint. We report rank and conversion separately so you can see which is improving and which is not. We tell you before you commit budget if a category's top position is defended by spend levels that make chasing it a negative-ROI decision. The algorithm changes without notice, and we adjust before the data shows a problem.

Shipped by the same team that did the diagnostic. 04 Ongoing: track Weekly bid and budget improvement against share of shelf. Monthly strategy review with full reporting.

sections.text: What you get Concrete deliverables. Every engagement produces the same set of outputs. You keep the baseline whether you continue or not. 01 A shelf position baseline you keep. Paid and organic positions, separated. Category competitive landscape. Signal audit. Whether or not you continue. 02 A written plan with prioritisation reasoning shown. Not a list of campaign ideas. Why each item, in what order, and what it is expected to move. 03 A weekly tracked report against the baseline. Share of shelf, split paid and organic, tracked against conversion. Changes signalled, not buried. 04 One team, not an account layer. The people who ran the audit are the people who manage the campaigns. No handoffs, no dropped context.

shoppable-ai-search.title: Shoppable AI search: the battle for share of generated sentence | Inflexion
shoppable-ai-search.body_text: Shoppable AI search: the battle for share of generated sentence | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us AI Discovery / Commerce Shoppable AI search: the battle for share of generated sentence Dunnhumby identifies the birth of shoppable AI search where brands battle for share of generated sentence. The focus is on summarising content for AI ingestion. 19 September 2026 · 8 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / The shift from shelf to sentence 02 / How AI search becomes shoppable 03 / Content that gets ingested 04 / Strategy for the generated sentence For decades, retail media has been about the shelf. Physical shelf. Digital shelf. Algorithmic shelf. The unit of competition was placement. Position one. Endcap. Sponsored product slot. Dunnhumby's 2025 retail tech trends identify a new unit: the generated sentence. In 2025, brands and retailers will start to battle for "share of generated sentence" as consumer adoption of AI search accelerates. The focus is on summarising content for AI ingestion and the recommendation mechanisms needed for content-rich product discovery. This is not a metaphor. When a shopper asks an AI assistant "What running shoes work for wide feet?" the assistant generates a sentence: "For wide feet, the New Balance 1080v13 and Hoka Clifton 9 are frequently recommended for their wide toe boxes and accommodating fit." The brands mentioned in that sentence win the share of generated sentence. The brands not mentioned do not exist in that shopping moment. 01. The shift from shelf to sentence. The shelf is a constrained physical or digital space. The generated sentence is an unconstrained semantic space. The shelf has finite slots. The sentence has finite attention. The competition has moved from placement to mention. On Marketing's October 2025 survey found that 90 percent of people read Google AI Overviews when provided. More than half read them most of the time. The AI Overview is the new shelf. The generated sentence is the new placement. HubSpot's State of AEO in 2026 report found that nearly half of surveyed marketers say they have personally made a business purchase decision based primarily on brand information they first discovered in AI-generated answers. AI referral traffic converts at 11.4 percent compared to 5.3 percent for organic search. Intent is the differentiator. The shelf is a place where products are displayed. The sentence is where products are recommended. 02. How AI search becomes shoppable. Shoppable AI search operates at three layers: Layer 1: Content ingestion. The AI system needs structured, extractable content. Product specifications, comparison tables, review summaries, use-case guides, FAQ pages. The content must be structured so the model can parse it, extract the answer, and cite the source. Layer 2: Recommendation mechanisms. The model weights authority, relevance, clarity, and freshness. Authority comes from earned media citations, brand mentions across trusted sources, and entity recognition. Relevance comes from direct answers to specific questions. Clarity comes from extractable structure. Freshness comes from recent content updates. Layer 3: Transaction enablement. Target, Etsy, Walmart, and Instacart have all enabled checkout in ChatGPT. One-click buy without leaving the chat. The generated sentence becomes the purchase trigger. "For wide feet, the New Balance 1080v13..." becomes a clickable link that completes the purchase in the chat interface. The focus is on summarising content for AI ingestion and the recommendation mechanisms needed for content-rich product discovery. The adoption of AI search gives retailers a new way to capture digital customer journey signals. 03. Content that gets ingested. Not all content is equal. The model prefers: Comparison content. ChatGPT cites comparison content at a 95 percent rate. "New Balance 1080v13 vs Hoka Clifton 9 for wide feet" is the content the model wants. Documentation and resources. ChatGPT cites documentation at 86 percent. Technical specifications, fit guides, use-case matrices. Blog content. Google AI Overviews cite blog content at 42 percent. Perplexity cites blog posts and informative articles at 80 percent. Pages with quotes or statistics. Pages with quotes or statistics have 30 to 40 percent higher visibility in AI answers. Earned media. Muck Rack reports 84 percent of AI citations come from earned media. Owned content and paid sources account for smaller shares. Self-published content may provide less independent corroboration. The content strategy shifts from keyword targeting to question answering. Map the questions shoppers ask. Create content that directly answers each question. Structure it for extraction. Distribute it to the sources the model trusts. The model does not read your keyword strategy. It reads your answers to questions. 04. Strategy for the generated sentence. The battle for share of generated sentence requires a different playbook: Map the question set. Not keywords. Questions. "What running shoes work for wide feet?" "Which television works in bright rooms?" "What wireless earbuds suit Zoom calls?" Each question defines the content you need. Build the answer library. One page per question. Direct answer in the first paragraph. Supporting evidence below. Structured for extraction: FAQ schema, comparison tables, specification lists, review summaries. Earn the citations. The model cites what others say about you. Digital PR for AEO earns coverage in the sources models already cite. Source mapping, entity building, citation-weighted outreach. The source map is the targeting list. Structure the entity. Wikipedia, Crunchbase, G2, industry directories, analyst listings. The sources models use to answer "who is company X." Audit every reference source. Fix inconsistencies. Build a complete entity footprint. Activate community presence. Reddit, Quora, YouTube, Stack Exchange, niche forums. Community content is a growing share of AI citations. Answer real questions with natural language. The model reads the text around your brand name. Track share of generated sentence. Not rankings. Not traffic. The proportion of a defined buyer prompt set, across a defined set of models, in which your brand appears in the generated sentence. Position within the sentence. Sentiment of the mention. Consistency across models. The metric is fixed and published. The number means something because the questions did not change. index.body_text: Inflexion: Marketing for the AI era Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Full-service marketing for the AI era AI has fundamentally changed the customer journey. Most brands are building for where it used to be. Full-service capability across discovery, media, retail and data, with AI in the operating model Run the baseline → 900M Weekly ChatGPT users Source: OpenAI, Feb 2026 69% Zero-click searches Source: Similarweb, 2025 $1.1B GEO market (2026) Source: Dimension Market Research 82% Citations from earned media Source: Muck Rack, 2025 86.7% Business queries trigger AI Peec AI, April 2026 $2.5B OpenAI's projected 2026 ad revenue eMarketer, 2026 The economics have changed EXECUTION More people producing more work AI makes execution abundant. EXPERTISE Specialist knowledge locked inside large teams AI puts extraordinary capability in everyone's hands. JUDGEMENT More analysis. More dashboards. More outputs. Knowing what matters becomes the competitive advantage. TEAM Large teams. Multiple layers. Endless hand-offs. Small, senior teams with AI as leverage. AI doesn't replace expertise. It amplifies it. The organisations that win with AI won't be the ones with the most tools. They'll be the ones that know where to apply them, how to redesign the work around them, and when not to trust them. That's the Inflexion model: experienced people directly in the problem, using AI to accelerate research, analysis, creation and execution, while applying the thing AI cannot reliably provide: context, experience and judgement. Human judgement. AI leverage. Measurable outcomes. How we work One process. Strategy first, then speed. 01 Understand The objective and the overarching strategy, not a channel brief. What has to be true for this to count as a win. 02 Accelerate AI compresses the research and onboarding, account audits, market and competitor analysis, into days instead of weeks. 03 Codify The agreed objective gets built into the system: the rules and automations that run the work, not a slide that gets forgotten after kickoff. 04 Sprint Two weeks, one outcome, executed against that system. 05 Scale What proves out runs through the same system at full budget. What doesn't gets cut before it costs more. What we do Six disciplines. One team. I. AEO Become the source AI models cite Structured content, entity signals and ongoing diagnostics across Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini. We track not just whether you're mentioned, but what's said about you. +40% visibility lift Princeton, KDD 2024 How citation works → II. SEO Still the largest channel, still needs the basics done right Technical fixes, site structure and content built properly. The same foundations that earn rankings also determine whether AI models can read and trust your pages. 53% of traffic still organic Branch, 2026 Where SEO fits now → III. Retail Media One strategy across every retailer you sell through Amazon, Walmart, Instacart, Target and the rest, planned and reported together instead of as separate accounts, with paid spend tracked apart from organic rank. 5x AI referral conversion Seer Interactive, 2025 Whitepaper How the shelf works → IV. AI-improved Media Bids and budgets that move in real time, not on a monthly call Algorithmic buying already sets price and pacing across most channels. The work that matters now is feeding it clean data and deciding what it should prioritise. 15.3% of budgets already AI-directed Gartner, 2026 How AI media works → V. Strategic Consultancy Rebuild the team around what AI can't do AI has absorbed most of the execution agencies used to staff for. We restructure around judgment instead: fewer people, closer to the data, making the calls that actually move results. 73% of CMOs: AI now does what needed a 15-20 person team Industry survey, 2026 The operating model → VI. Data & Measurement One clean, trusted dataset, not seven disconnected tools Attribution and reporting that ties citations, retail rank and campaign performance back to a single source of truth, so decisions aren't built on bad data. Avg. business uses 7 tools to read its own data ClickZ/Fospha See the framework → The old funnel isn't coming back. Find out where you stand. An AI visibility audit across the answer engines and the algorithmic shelf. You keep the baseline either way. Run the baseline → Marketing for the AI inflection. technical-geo.body_text:
Technical GEO | AI Crawler improvement | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us III. Technical GEO
AI visibility
AI crawlers see your raw HTML, not your marketing. AI models don't render JavaScript. They read the static HTML your server returns. If your content loads client-side, product descriptions, article body, spec sheets, it is invisible to the systems making buying recommendations. Run the technical audit → What we fix 86.7% AI Overviews on business queries Source: Peec AI, April 2026 4 in 5 Brands have AI-unreadable sites Source: Inflexion audits, 2025–2026 7 Technical dimensions of GEO Source: Inflexion framework 83% Citations from outside top 10 Source: ConvertMate, 2026 The barrier 4 in 5 brands Most brands have websites AI crawlers cannot read. 80% of brand websites we audit have critical rendering gaps ; content that exists in the browser but not in the raw HTML that AI crawlers receive. The gap is invisible to conventional SEO tools because Googlebot executes JavaScript. AI crawlers do not. AI crawlers, the bots that feed GPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, and every other major model, operate fundamentally differently from search engine crawlers. Googlebot runs a full Chromium browser. Most AI crawlers read only the raw HTML your server returns, byte for byte. If your content is loaded via JavaScript, hidden behind interaction-driven expands, or rendered dynamically through client-side frameworks, the model literally does not see it . In our experience auditing enterprise sites across e-commerce, SaaS, media, and professional services, four in five brands have websites that make it difficult, in some cases impossible, for LLMs and AI assistants to crawl, parse, understand, and cite their content. The technical layer is the invisible blocker to AI visibility. And it is the one most agencies overlook entirely. What gets lost JS-only Product descriptions, pricing tables, spec sheets loaded via React/Vue/Angular Hidden Tabbed content, accordions, "read more" expands, everything behind interaction Unstructured Rendered text with no schema, no entity markup, model can't verify context What we fix Seven technical dimensions of AI discoverability. Each dimension is audited, measured against our proprietary scoring framework, and remediated with a documented before/after. This is a diagnostic pipeline, not only a checklist. 01. Crawler access Control which AI bots can reach your content. Most robots.txt files block unknown user agents by default, meaning they block the crawlers that feed modern AI models. We audit and configure access so CCBot, GPTBot, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, and emerging crawlers can reach your pages without exposing sensitive paths. Average blocked AI crawlers found: 4 to 7 per site 02. Server-side rendering Content must exist in the initial HTML response. AI crawlers do not execute JavaScript. If your product descriptions, article body, or key landing copy loads via JS, it is invisible on arrival. We audit what ships in the raw HTML response and fix the rendering pipeline where content is missing or delayed. Pages with SSR gaps: ~65% of e-commerce sites 03. Schema & entities Tell the model what your page is about. Structured data is how models disambiguate meaning and verify entity relationships. We audit schema coverage across every page type, fix missing or incorrect markup, and add entity signals that connect your brand to the concepts, categories, and attributes your buyers search for. Schema coverage lift: 20% → 85%+ within 6 weeks 04. Sitemap & crawl budget Make sure the important pages are found first. Most sitemaps reflect org-chart structure, not customer intent. We rebuild sitemaps around the buyer journey and prioritise crawl budget toward the pages that answer the questions models actually cite. AI crawlers have limited depth, so every wasted crawl is a missed citation. Sitemap efficiency improvement: 3 to 5x on citable pages 05. LLMs.txt A machine-readable guide to your most citable pages. The llms.txt standard gives AI crawlers a curated entry point to your most important content. We create and maintain one per site; it is a relatively low-effort measure that complements the fundamentals, giving models a direct path to your highest-value pages. Adopted by 72% of new AI crawlers (2025 to 2026) 06. Page rendering audit Test what AI crawlers actually see when they visit. We fetch every important page as a raw-text AI crawler would: no JS, no rendering, and compare it to what Googlebot and a full browser see. The delta between the two is your technical gap, quantified per page. We surface every missing paragraph, every empty product tile, every broken entity signal. Average gap: 40 to 60% of page content invisible 07. Entity positioning Control the narrative around your brand's core entities. Models construct a relationship graph between entities: brands, products, attributes, topics, people. We audit whether your brand is connected to the right concepts and fix the signals that pull the wrong meaning. If your brand shares entity space with competitors or unrelated topics, we surface it and fix it. Entity misalignment detected on ~58% of sites Technical audit scorecard Seven dimensions. One diagnostic. Each dimension is scored 0–100 on a page-level crawl. The radar profile shows where your site is AI-ready and where rendering gaps block citation. Technical GEO Readiness Profile Radar chart of the 7 technical dimensions. Larger area = more AI-crawler-friendly. Your Brand vs Industry Average vs Best-in-Class. Mock data, replace with live audit API data. Axes: Crawler Access, SSR Coverage, Schema & Entities, Sitemap Efficiency, LLMs.txt, Rendering Audit, Entity Positioning. What the Browser Sees vs What AI Crawls Slopegraph comparing content element visibility between full browser render and raw HTML AI crawler response. Lines slope down = content invisible to AI. Mock data, replace with live page-level rendering audit. Each line = one content element type. Schema Coverage Over Remediation Sprint Area chart showing page-level schema coverage improving across a 6-week remediation. Shaded region = gap from baseline to target (85%+). Mock data, replace with live schema audit progression. Target: 85%+ schema coverage on citable pages. AI Crawler Access: Allowed vs Blocked Radial bar showing which major AI crawlers can access your site. Green = allowed; orange = blocked in robots.txt; gray = unknown/untested. Average enterprise blocks 4–7. Mock data, replace with live robots.txt + crawl test results. Crawlers: GPTBot, CCBot, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, BingPreview, Applebot, Anthropic-AI. The audit process We fetch what AI crawlers actually see. Every engagement starts with a page-level rendering audit. We fetch each important page as a raw-text AI crawler would, no JavaScript, no rendering, and compare it against what a full browser sees. The delta between the two is the technical gap, quantified per page. Missing paragraphs, empty product tiles, missing schema: each surfaces with a specific remediation. Most enterprise sites show a 40% to 60% gap between browser-rendered content and the raw HTML that AI crawlers receive. Fixing the gap does not guarantee citation, but the best content written is content the model cannot read. The technical layer is the foundation. Run the technical audit → Why it matters now AI crawler compatibility is the new mobile-friendliness. When Google introduced mobile-friendliness as a ranking signal in 2015, a large part of the web became effectively invisible overnight. The same structural shift is happening right now with AI crawlers, except the stakes are fundamentally different: invisible does not mean a lower ranking. It means not being in the answer at all . 73% of AI answers cite from fewer than 3 domains. If your site is excluded, it does not rank; it does not exist in the answer at all. 3 to 5 years window to act before AI-native citations become a standard competitive factor across every vertical. 01 JS rendering gaps hide entire product lines from AI. If your product catalogue loads via JavaScript, AI crawlers see an empty page. Every SKU, every description, every spec: invisible to the systems making buying recommendations. ~65% of enterprise e-commerce sites affected 02 Missing schema blocks entity understanding. Without structured data, models cannot reliably connect your brand to the topics, categories, and attributes your buyers search for. You may be in the model's index but mapped to nothing useful, or worse, mapped to competitors. 42% of sites have zero schema markup 03 Robots.txt overblocking shuts out AI entirely. The default position for many enterprise sites is to block unknown bots via robots.txt. That now includes the bots that feed the answer engines your buyers use every day. We find 4 to 7 AI crawlers blocked per site on average. 30% of Index of Millions sites block GPTBot Is your site built for AI crawlers? A technical rendering audit shows you exactly what AI models can and cannot read on your site, page by page, element by element. We deliver a scored report with a ranked remediation list. Free initial scan (up to 25 pages) 48-hour turnaround No commitment required Run the technical audit → Technical GEO for AI discovery. amazon-rufus-sponsored-prompts.body_text: Amazon Rufus and the sponsored prompt evolution | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Retail Media / Amazon Amazon Rufus and the sponsored prompt evolution Amazon Rufus reached 250 million monthly users. Then came sponsored prompts. Here is what the shift from search to conversational commerce means for retail media. 19 September 2026 · 9 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / From assistant to ad platform 02 / The mechanics of sponsored prompts 03 / What this changes for retail media 04 / How to prepare your catalogue Retail media has always been about placement. Bid on keywords. Win the impression. Measure the return. Amazon Rufus changes the unit of competition. Launched in early 2024, Rufus reached 250 million monthly users by late 2025. Shoppers using Rufus demonstrate 60 percent higher purchase intent compared to traditional search. The assistant does not just retrieve products. It synthesises recommendations from product specifications, technical attributes, customer review sentiment, and comparative analysis. In November 2024, Amazon introduced sponsored prompts into Rufus conversations. The mechanics are deceptively simple. Product-level prompts surface when users discuss specific categories. A query about televisions might trigger a follow-up suggestion: "Would you like to explore Samsung's latest models?" Brand-level prompts focus on category discovery. The prompts draw on product specifications, technical attributes, and customer review sentiment. This is not a new ad format layered on top of search. It is a new discovery surface where the ad is the answer. 01. From assistant to ad platform. Rufus was not built as an ad platform. It was built as a shopping assistant trained on Amazon's product catalogue, customer reviews, community Q&A, and information from across the web. Amazon says shoppers use it for product research, comparisons, and recommendations. The important detail is the input. Rufus does not need another banner. It needs usable evidence. The shift happened because the assistant reached scale. 250 million monthly users. 60 percent higher purchase intent. Amazon reports that shoppers using Rufus demonstrate stronger intent signals than traditional search users. The assistant became a discovery surface too valuable to leave unmonetised. The sponsored prompt does not look like an ad. It looks like a helpful follow-up. "Would you like to explore Samsung's latest models?" feels like the assistant being helpful. The commercial intent is embedded in the conversational flow. The ad is no longer a placement. The ad is the suggestion the assistant makes. 02. The mechanics of sponsored prompts. Amazon introduced two types of sponsored prompts in November 2024. Product-level prompts. These surface when users discuss specific product categories. A query about televisions triggers: "Would you like to explore Samsung's latest models?" The prompts draw on product specifications, technical attributes, and customer review sentiment. The assistant is not just matching keywords. It is matching the conversation context to product attributes. Brand-level prompts. These focus on category discovery rather than specific items. A user asking "What should I look for in a running shoe?" might receive a brand-level suggestion guiding them toward a specific manufacturer's range. The prompt draws on broader brand authority signals, category expertise, and comparative positioning. Both prompt types share a critical dependency: the quality of the underlying product data. If specifications are incomplete, if review sentiment is negative, if attributes are missing, the sponsored prompt will not surface or will surface with weak evidence. The bid does not control the prompt. The evidence controls the prompt. 03. What this changes for retail media. The unit of competition has moved from the keyword to the conversation context. In traditional retail media, you bid on "wireless earbuds." In Rufus, the shopper asks: "What wireless earbuds work well for Zoom calls?" The assistant synthesises a recommendation based on microphone quality, battery life, comfort for long calls, and review sentiment around call clarity. A sponsored prompt might surface: "Would you like to explore Jabra's latest models?" because Jabra's product data includes detailed microphone specifications and positive review sentiment around call quality. The brands that win are not the ones with the highest bids. They are the ones with the most complete, accurate, and conversion-relevant product evidence. This extends beyond Amazon. Dunnhumby's 2025 retail tech trends identify the birth of "shoppable AI search" where brands and retailers battle for "share of generated sentence." The focus is on summarising content for AI ingestion and the recommendation mechanisms needed for content-rich product discovery. The shelf is no longer a place where products are ranked. It is where the assistant makes a case for them. 04. How to prepare your catalogue for conversational discovery. The sponsored prompt does not appear because you bid higher. It appears because your product evidence matches the conversation context. Start with a question audit. Map the questions shoppers ask in your category. Not keywords. Questions. "What wireless earbuds work for Zoom calls?" "Which running shoes suit wide feet?" "What television works in bright rooms?" Each question defines the evidence the assistant needs. Then audit your product data against those questions. Do your specifications include microphone frequency response? Do your attributes include fit type for wide feet? Do your review summaries mention call clarity? The assistant cannot recommend what it cannot verify. Review velocity matters. A product with 50 recent positive reviews about call quality will outrank a product with 500 old reviews about sound quality. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. Availability and fulfilment feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is in place. The assistant factors in delivery promises when synthesising recommendations. Separate paid position from earned position in your reporting. A sponsored prompt that surfaces because of strong product evidence is different from one that surfaces only because of budget. Track both. The prompt does not need a higher bid. The prompt needs better evidence. Amazon's advertising revenue reached $56.2 billion in 2024, pacing a $69 billion run-rate. The company's AI Creative Studio, layered with Nova foundation models in late 2024, converts a single hero image into dozens of video variations in minutes. Prime Video now has an average monthly ad-supported reach of more than 315 million viewers globally. The flywheel is clear: more advertisers create more data. More data makes the system smarter. A smarter system gets better results, which encourages more spend. But the flywheel only spins if the product evidence is there. The brands that invest in complete, accurate, conversion-relevant product data will be the ones the assistant recommends. The brands that treat Rufus as another bid surface will be the ones the assistant skips. Sources Grocery Doppio, Amazon Ads: How a $56B Engine Is Reshaping Grocery Media . Marketing Dive, Trendline on Retail Media Networks . Dunnhumby, AI, automation, and authenticity: our retail tech trends for 2025 . Audit your shelf position before the assistant changes it. We separate paid position, organic position, and the product signals behind both. Audit your shelf position Amazon / Rufus prompts. amazon-ai-creative-studio.title: Amazon AI Creative Studio and the collapse of production timelines | Inflexion
amazon-ai-creative-studio.body_text: Amazon AI Creative Studio and the collapse of production timelines | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Amazon / AI Creative Amazon AI Creative Studio and the collapse of production timelines Amazon Nova foundation models convert a single hero image into dozens of video variations in minutes. What used to cost five figures and six weeks now runs on autopilot. 19 September 2026 · 8 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / What the studio does 02 / The flywheel effect 03 / What this means for creative strategy 04 / How to prepare your assets Creative production has always been the bottleneck. A mid-tier CPG brand spends five figures and six weeks to produce a single video asset. The brief goes to an agency. The agency storyboards. The production crew shoots. Post-production edits. Revisions cycle. The asset finally ships. Late 2024, Amazon layered its Nova foundation models onto an AI Creative Studio. The studio converts a single hero image into dozens of six-second video or audio variations in minutes. The output plugs straight into Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, or Streaming TV campaigns. The economics have inverted. What cost five figures and six weeks now runs on autopilot. The constraint has shifted from production capacity to asset strategy. 01. What the studio does. The AI Creative Studio is not a design tool. It is a generation engine. Input a single hero image. The Nova foundation models generate dozens of six-second video variations, audio variations, and static creative sized for different placements: Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, Sponsored Display, and Streaming TV. The studio handles aspect ratio adaptation, brand-safe framing, text overlay placement, and platform-specific formatting. The output is broadcast-ready and policy-compliant by default. For a mid-tier CPG brand, this eliminates the agency production cycle entirely. The creative team uploads the hero asset. The studio generates the variation set. The media team selects the best performers and launches. The bottleneck has moved from production to selection. 02. The flywheel effect. Amazon's advertising revenue reached $56.2 billion in 2024, pacing a $69 billion run-rate. Three factors drove the climb: opening Prime Video to advertisers, expanding Sponsored Products and Display across Fresh aisles, and a data advantage that lets brands see transaction-level return on ad spend within 48 hours. The AI Creative Studio adds a fourth accelerant. Lower creative cost means more advertisers test more variations. More variations generate more performance data. More data makes the system smarter at predicting what creative works. A smarter system gets better results, which encourages more spend. Prime Video now has an average monthly ad-supported reach of more than 315 million viewers globally, up from 200 million in April 2024. Amazon has integrated other publishers into its platform and claims to be the only place advertisers can access all premium streaming TV and audio under one roof. The flywheel is clear: lower creative cost brings more advertisers. More advertisers create more data. More data makes the system smarter. Better results encourage more spend. Creative automation is not a feature. It is the fourth flywheel accelerant. 03. What this means for creative strategy. When creative production is no longer the constraint, the strategic question changes. It is no longer "what can we afford to produce?" It is "what should we test?" The brands that win will not be the ones with the biggest production budgets. They will be the ones with the best testing frameworks. This means: creative strategy becomes hypothesis design. Each variation tests a specific variable: hook, value proposition, visual style, call to action, audio treatment. The media team runs the test. The data reveals the winner. The winning variable informs the next hypothesis. It also means: brand governance must adapt. When the studio generates dozens of variations in minutes, the approval workflow cannot be a weekly review meeting. Brands need pre-approved brand guidelines that the studio operates within. aeo.body_text: Answer Engine Optimisation: Getting Cited by AI | Inflexion Home Contact us AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Answer Engine Optimisation Get your brand cited when AI gives the answer. ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity reach billions of users with AI answers. Brands cited in those answers can gain discovery. Brands that are not cited miss that route to discovery. Run the citation audit → Why AEO matters 900M Weekly ChatGPT users Source: OpenAI, Feb 2026 69% Zero-click searches Source: Similarweb, 2025 40% GEO visibility lift Source: Princeton/KDD, 2024 83% Citations outside top 10 Source: ConvertMate, 2026 The AI visibility stack The problem Search became answers. Your SEO didn't follow. Answer Engine Optimisation is not rebadged SEO. The signals differ in several important ways: keyword density matters less than factual clarity; backlink volume matters less than citation frequency across authoritative sources; page speed matters less than whether your content can be parsed into a direct answer. We have measured brands ranking first on Google that are entirely absent from the AI answer to the same query. Search engines work from a list of blue links. Answer engines generate a direct response. The useful measure is share of answer, not share of clicks. The mechanics of earning that answer are specific: factual clarity, entity structure, source authority and citation frequency all matter more than keyword density or backlink volume. Our AEO framework Five dimensions that affect each other. We structure AEO around five interconnected dimensions. You cannot fix citation without addressing structure, or structure without addressing signal authority. C1 Clarity Does the model understand what you are saying? We restructure content so the model can extract the answer directly: one question per page, concise answers, clear entity relationships marked up in schema. C2 Authority Models cite sources other sources cite. We map which outlets, research papers, forums, and data sets carry authority in your category, then build a prioritised plan for earning citations there. C3 Structure Schema, headings, entity relationships, the scaffolding that tells a model what a page is about. Without it, even good content gets ignored because the model cannot categorise it reliably. C4 Freshness Models weight recent content differently. A page from 2021 is nearly invisible even if still correct. We build content programmes that keep the model's view of your category updated. C5 Measurement Share of answer across models. Whether you are named, at what position, in response to which prompts: tracked month over month against a fixed, published baseline. How AEO works Content built for extraction, not ranking. Traditional SEO writes for the searcher. AEO writes for the model. The difference shows up in how the page is structured: each question gets its own page, the answer sits in the first paragraph, supporting detail follows, and schema marks up every entity the model needs to verify. This is not a content-quantity play. A single page that directly answers one buyer question, with the right entity signals and source authority, can outperform dozens of pages written for keyword variation. The model does not need volume. It needs something it can cite with confidence. Most categories are under-improved for AI citation right now. The window closes as more brands catch up. Run the citation audit → What you get Concrete deliverables. 01 A prompt set audit. A fixed set of buyer questions run across four to six models. You see exactly where you are cited, where competitors are cited, and where neither of you is. 02 A source authority map. The outlets, forums, papers, and data sources models trust in your category: ranked by influence, with a prioritised plan for earning citations there. 03 AEO-improved content. Pages restructured or written from scratch to maximise citability: one question per page, clear answer structure, schema that signals entity relationships. 04 Monthly tracking. Share of answer with position and citation status, tracked month over month. The baseline is fixed and published: the number means something. Find out whether AI knows your brand. A citation audit across the models your buyers actually use. You keep the baseline either way. Run the citation audit → Answer Engine Optimisation built on evidence. ai-discovery.title: AI Discovery | Getting Cited by AI | Inflexion
ai-discovery.body_text: AI Discovery | Getting Cited by AI | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us AI Discovery Getting cited by AI is not the same as ranking. Models don't read your SERP position. They read your content. We measure whether you appear in the answer, across the models your buyers actually use. Run the prompt set audit → How we diagnose The AI visibility stack 01. The real mechanics How AI models decide who to cite: and what that means for your content strategy. When a user asks a model a question, the model does not search Google and read the top result. It generates an answer from its training data and, where retrieval is available, draws on external sources. Models reward four things: authority (how often a source is cited by other sources the model trusts), relevance (whether the content directly answers the question being asked), clarity (whether the information is structured so the model can parse it), and freshness (how recent the content is). There is no position one through ten. There is being in the answer and not being in the answer . Brands that rank first on Google for a query are often absent from the AI answer to the same query, because models and search engines weigh signals differently. We have measured this gap across dozens of categories. It is larger than most marketing teams realise. This is why traditional SEO, built around keyword ranking, backlink volume and click-through rate, does not translate directly to AI citation. The work is adjacent but distinct. The skills overlap but the output metric is different. Some AEO services largely reproduce traditional SEO. The actual work is about being the clearest, most authoritative source on a specific question , not about filling a keyword gap. 02. The audit What we actually check when we check your AI visibility. Nobody can plan this without a baseline, and almost nobody has one. The diagnostic is deliberately specified tightly enough that you could commission it from someone else. The diagnostic includes an operational reading of the output and a plan that follows from it. 01 Prompt set construction. We build a set of buyer questions specific to your category, covering the arc from broad category awareness through to comparison and purchase-intent queries. We exclude brand-name searches: nobody discovers you by typing your name. The prompt set is published to you and fixed for the duration of the engagement. 02 Cross-model testing. The same prompt set run across four to six models, depending on what your buyers actually use. Models disagree more than expected: a brand well-cited in Claude can be absent from GPT, and neither pattern predicts Gemini or Perplexity. Testing one model gives a misleading picture. 03 Source mapping. When a model names a competitor, we trace what it drew from. This reveals which sources carry authority in your category: independent reviews, comparison tables, analyst reports, forum discussions. The source map can be one of the most actionable findings in the audit, because it tells you exactly where to build credibility. 04 Gap analysis and prioritisation. The baseline tells you two things: where you stand today, and what the category authority landscape looks like. The prioritised plan identifies which gaps are winnable within a quarter, which require longer investment, and which are structural constraints that cannot be engineered around. The output is a baseline document, not a pitch. You keep it whether or not you work with us. 03. The framework, applied Baseline. Build. Re-test. For discovery. Diagnose Keyword rankings Prompt set audit + source map Measure Organic traffic Share of answer, position, citation Run Content for ranking Content built to be cited, shipped by the team that ran the audit Some categories may offer relatively low-cost opportunities while citation work is still immature. That advantage may narrow as more brands catch up. See the full framework → 04. How we measure it Share of answer, tracked. Not traffic, not rankings. The metric Share of answer. The proportion of a defined buyer prompt set, across a defined set of models, in which your brand appears in the generated answer. Position within the answer is recorded, being named as the first recommendation is different from being mentioned in a list of three. The integrity The prompt set is fixed and published. We do not change the prompts without telling you and re-baselining. Changing the questions changes the number, and we want the number to mean something. The caveat This is not revenue. It is a leading indicator. Treat it the way share of search has been treated, an early signal that correlates with commercial outcomes, not a substitute for measuring them. Full measurement methodology → 05. The first quarter From standing start to first tracked movement. 01 Weeks 1–3: baseline Prompt set built, models tested, source map produced. Output is the baseline document you keep. 02 Weeks 4–6: plan Prioritised by what the baseline shows is winnable. Measurement agreed and instrumented before any content ships. 03 Weeks 7–12: build SEO foundations fixed, content written to be cited. Shipped by the same team that ran the diagnostic. 04 Ongoing: track Monthly re-run of the prompt set. Models change. So does the work. 06. Timeline and expectations AEO changes take time. Here is the timeline. 01 Month one: baseline and structural work. Prompt set built, models tested, source map produced. Content and technical foundations fixed. No citation movement expected yet. 02 Month two: first content ships. Pages restructured for citability. Schema deployed. Models re-crawl on their own schedule. Movement may begin but should not be assumed. 03 Month three and beyond: measured change. First meaningful citation movement typically appears. Continues compounding if the programme is maintained. Models drift, competitors respond; this is a tracked programme, not a project. Find out if AI even knows you exist. An AI visibility audit across the answer engines that matter to your category. You keep the baseline either way. Run the prompt set audit → AI Discovery services: AEO, visibility analytics, technical GEO, digital PR. ai-media.body_text: AI-Powered Media, Programmatic, CTV, and Automated Buying | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us AI-Powered Media 71% of ad spend is now algorithmic. Feed it the right signals. Programmatic display, CTV, streaming audio and digital out-of-home are now bought programmatically across many channels. The focus is to provide reliable data and define what systems should improve. Bids and budgets move in real time, not on a monthly call. Audit your media feed → How AI media works 71% Ad spend algorithmically driven Dentsu, 2026 $753B Global digital ad spend (2026) Business of Apps 15.3% Budgets already AI-directed Gartner, 2026 32% More conversions via AI campaigns Averi, 2025 The shift Media buying is now autonomous. The question is what the algorithm prioritises. In 2026, agentic AI does not just execute bids, it plans the media mix, allocates budget across channels, and adjusts in real time based on performance signals. The human role has shifted from "set the bid" to "design the objective function." ai-in-retail-media.title: AI in retail media: the shelf is becoming a decision system | Inflexion
ai-in-retail-media.body_text: AI in retail media: the shelf is becoming a decision system | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Retail media / AI commerce AI in retail media: the shelf is becoming a decision system Retail media began as sponsored placement. AI is making product data, reviews, price and conversion more important to what gets seen. 18 September 2026 · 12 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / The old shelf 02 / Three phases 03 / Decision system 04 / Five operating shifts 05 / What to measure 06 / The core idea Most retail media teams still manage the shelf as if it were a row of billboards. Pick a keyword, set a bid, buy an impression, report the return. That model is becoming incomplete. Retailers are adding AI to product discovery, campaign management, recommendations and customer service. Shoppers are asking questions in natural language. Agents are beginning to compare products on a person's behalf. Competition is shifting from the ad slot to the evidence behind the product. This does not make paid media irrelevant. It makes paid media more dependent on everything around it: product information, price, availability, reviews and the quality of the experience after the click. Treating AI only as a creative tool misses the change in how retail systems evaluate products. The better question is: what information does the retail system need in order to choose us? 01. The old shelf was bought. The new shelf is also evaluated. Retail media has always contained an algorithm. Amazon, Walmart, Instacart and other retailers have long used relevance, predicted performance and commercial value to decide which products appear where. Bidding only ever controlled one part of the equation. AI makes the equation more visible because the shopper may no longer begin with a short keyword. They may ask for a quiet dishwasher for a small kitchen, a running shoe for wet trails, or a birthday gift under a specific budget. The system has to interpret the need, find suitable products, compare trade-offs and explain the recommendation. Amazon's Rufus is an early public example. Launched in beta in February 2024 and later rolled out to US customers, Rufus uses Amazon's product catalogue, customer reviews, community questions and web information. Amazon says shoppers can use it for product research, comparisons and recommendations. The important detail is the input. Rufus does not need another banner. It needs usable evidence. The implications extend beyond Amazon. Deloitte's 2025 report on agentic commerce recorded increased AI referrals to US retail sites during 2025. The rate will change as measurement improves. The report points to more product research happening before shoppers reach a retailer's standard search results. The shelf is no longer only a place where products are ranked. It is where the retail system makes a case for them. 02. Three phases of retail media Phase one: placement The first retail media playbook borrowed from search advertising. Brands bought terms close to purchase, watched click-through rate and conversion, then adjusted bids. Teams tracked catalogue quality and feedback speed alongside click-through rate and conversion. Phase two: performance As the channel matured, teams added richer campaign structures, audience signals, retail data and incrementality questions. Retail media became a performance channel with its own version of attribution. That was a useful step, but it also encouraged teams to focus on the number visible in the ad console. Phase three: assisted choice AI adds a layer before the click. The system interprets a need and decides which products belong in the answer. It may use a product feed, reviews, delivery promise, price and external information. A product can have a strong ad position and still fail the recommendation if the underlying evidence is thin or contradictory. This phase can be described as evidence-led retail media. Evidence-led retail media means managing paid placement, product information and customer signals as one connected system. You still need media buying. You also need to make the product easy for a retailer, a shopping assistant and a customer to understand. 03. The two ground rules Ground rule one: the product feed is media infrastructure. Titles, attributes, images, descriptions, availability and fulfilment details are not background administration. They affect whether a product appears in a relevant comparison and remains a credible recommendation. Ground rule two: design for the decision, not the impression. An impression is a delivery event. A decision is a shopper choosing your product, or an agent retaining it as a credible option. The second outcome requires more than attention. It requires a coherent answer to the buyer's question. 04. Five operating shifts 1. Write product data for questions The old approach starts with a keyword list. The better approach starts with the questions that determine choice. What is it suitable for? Who should avoid it? How does it compare with the common alternative? What does the customer need to know about size, compatibility, ingredients, noise, delivery or maintenance? This is not an invitation to fill every field with copy. It is a request for precise, consistent product evidence. The same claim should not appear as a vague promise in the title and a different claim in the specification table. AI systems compare patterns across the information available to them, so contradictions can affect how a listing is assessed. Operating lesson: build a question set for each category, then map every answer to a source field, a proof point and a customer outcome. 2. Separate paid position from earned position Blended ROAS can make a weak product look healthy. If a product ranks well only when sponsored, the report should say so. If organic position improves after a campaign changes traffic quality or conversion, that should be visible too. Report at least four views: paid position, organic position, conversion by traffic source and availability during the measurement period. The exact dashboard will vary by retailer, but the principle holds. Do not let the media console become the only version of reality. Operating lesson: every weekly report should show what was bought, what was earned and what the product did when people arrived. 3. Treat creative as structured evidence Retail creative still needs to earn attention, but its job is broader than that. Images and video answer questions quickly. A comparison chart can remove doubt. A clear pack shot can confirm size or format. A demonstration can make a claim believable. AI shopping systems change the value of this work because they need reliable signals across the listing, not a single headline. Creative, copy and product attributes should tell the same story. When they do, the customer gets a clearer explanation and the listing presents fewer conflicting signals. Operating lesson: brief creative against the decision it must support, not only the placement where it will appear. 4. Feed the algorithm better traffic Retail media teams often treat off-platform traffic as a separate acquisition line. That misses the relationship between traffic quality and retail performance. If external activity brings people who are likely to buy, the resulting conversion and sales history may affect the product's future position. If it brings cheap clicks with little intent, the signal may be less useful. Retail media, paid social, search, creator activity and product data all affect what happens on the product detail page. The retailer sees the behaviour that follows the visit. Operating lesson: assess external traffic by what it teaches the retail system, as well as by its immediate cost per acquisition. 5. Build a measurement layer above the platforms Retailers will continue to improve their own reporting. Brands still need a view across the system. That view should connect share of shelf, paid and organic rank, availability, price, reviews, traffic source and conversion. AI makes this more important because the path from question to purchase is harder to observe. A customer may ask an assistant for a shortlist, visit one retailer, return through a different device and buy later. Perfect attribution is unlikely. Better diagnosis is possible. Use directional evidence and label its limits. Track changes in recommendation presence, referral quality, product visibility and conversion. Keep a record of catalogue changes and retailer updates so that performance changes can be compared with those events. Operating lesson: measure the conditions that make demand possible, not only the last event you can attribute. 05. What AI will not fix AI can make weak retail media faster. It can create more variants, adjust more bids and produce more reports. It cannot decide whether the product deserves to win without reliable inputs. It will not solve a product that is out of stock, badly reviewed, overpriced for its category or unclear about its use. It will not make a contradictory listing trustworthy. It will not turn a blended metric into a useful one. More automation increases the impact of poor foundations because the system can act on poor information at scale. 06. The core idea The retail media playbook is moving through three stages: placement, performance and assisted choice. The next model is evidence-led retail media. The formula is simple: Useful product data + credible customer signals + paid distribution + measurement that separates what was bought from what was earned. Start by mapping the questions shoppers ask in your category. Check whether your product pages answer them consistently. Separate paid and organic position. Then connect media decisions to the conditions that shape the retail algorithm. AI will change the interface again. Teams that track the evidence beneath the interface can adapt as the interface changes. It requires a coherent answer to the buyer's question. 04. Five operating shifts 1. Write product data for questions The old approach starts with a keyword list. The better approach starts with the questions that determine choice. What is it suitable for? Who should avoid it? How does it compare with the common alternative? What does the customer need to know about size, compatibility, ingredients, noise, delivery or maintenance? This is not an invitation to fill every field with copy. It is a request for precise, consistent product evidence. The same claim should not appear as a vague promise in the title and a different claim in the specification

Pick a keyword, set a bid, buy an impression, report the return. That model is becoming incomplete. Retailers are adding AI to product discovery, campaign management, recommendations and customer service. Shoppers are asking questions in natural language. Agents are beginning to compare products on a person's behalf. Competition is shifting from the ad slot to the evidence behind the product. This does not make paid media irrelevant.
