agentic-media-buying.body_text: Agentic media buying: from dashboards to autonomous execution | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Media / Agentic AI Agentic media buying: from dashboards to autonomous execution AI agents are replacing channel-by-channel media buying with portfolio-based coordination. The shift from dashboard-driven management to continuous execution. 19 September 2026 · 9 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / The dashboard problem 02 / What agents actually do 03 / The infrastructure shift 04 / Governance in an agentic world For years, media buying has been dashboard-driven. Teams pull reports. Interpret what happened. Make decisions. Execute changes. Wait for the next report. The cycle is monthly at best, weekly at most. Agentic AI changes the cycle time. CommerceIQ's Ally AI agents now handle repetitive, high-volume operational tasks across sales, digital shelf, content, and retail media. The platform deploys agents for Shelf, Media, Sales, and Content. Media agents improve retail media performance using 50-plus retail signals at 40 times the scale of traditional rules-based campaign management. The shift is structural. Retail teams manage thousands of SKUs, optimize content, run retail media, and manage pricing and inventory across multiple retailers. Human teams cannot keep up. Currently, most teams spend much of their time pulling reports to interpret what happened. AI becomes valuable when it can understand the why and take immediate action. 01. The dashboard problem. Dashboards show what happened. They do not show what to do. A human reads the dashboard, forms a hypothesis, decides on an action, and executes it. The latency between insight and action is measured in days or weeks. Meanwhile, the algorithmic environment moves in real time. Bids adjust. Budgets pace. Competitors react. Inventory changes. The dashboard is always describing a past state. Scope3 describes the future as agent-to-agent media buying: AI agents replacing channel-by-channel media buying with portfolio-based coordination. The Unified Context Protocol, Advertising Context Protocol, and Agentic RTB Framework give AI agents a shared framework to communicate and collaborate. Early pilots are underway. Butler/Till is testing a media activation agent with Scope3, targeting a 40 percent cost reduction in media plan execution. The economics are shifting from human-operated dashboards to agent-operated execution. The dashboard describes the past. The agent acts in the present. 02. What agents actually do. Current genAI tools generate copy, suggest bids, and surface insights. Agentic AI is different. It is defined by independent decision-making, goal-oriented behaviour, and complex task execution without continuous human input. CommerceIQ's Ally AI agents demonstrate the pattern: Shelf Agent monitors content, availability, assortment, reviews, and search (CAARS) to create branded insight packs with recommended actions in seconds. Media Agent improves retail media performance using 50-plus retail signals at 40 times the scale of traditional rules-based campaign management. Retail media agents execute thousands of changes per day compared to the limited volume typical of manual or agency-led workflows. Sales Agent and Content Agent handle their respective domains with the same pattern: continuous monitoring, hypothesis generation, and autonomous execution within defined guardrails. The agents connect content, retail media, search, inventory, and demand data across systems. They do not just report on the data. They act on it. 03. The infrastructure shift. Agentic media buying requires new infrastructure. EMARKETER notes that the Unified Context Protocol (UCP), Advertising Context Protocol (AdCP), and Agentic RTB Framework (ARTF) give AI agents a shared framework to communicate and collaborate. This is not a feature upgrade. It is a system-level rebuild. Five shifts the industry is making in 2026: From channel-by-channel to portfolio-based coordination. From human-paced to real-time decisioning. From rules-based to goal-oriented control. From dashboard-driven to agent-driven execution. From siloed data to unified context. The first deliverable on every engagement is now a clean, unified data layer that every channel reads from. Most brands have seven disconnected tools producing conflicting signals. The first deliverable is a clean, unified data layer that every channel reads from. Clean first-party data is the fuel. Agentic AI is the engine. The work that matters is feeding the engine the right signals and defining what it should prioritise. The infrastructure is not the platform. The infrastructure is the data layer the agents share. 04. Governance in an agentic world. Nearly 80 percent of retail teams say they are open to reallocating agency budgets to AI agents if recommendations are transparent and human teams retain final control. The governance model must evolve. From human approval of every decision to human approval of the objective function. The agent works within the objective function. The human sets the objective function: target ROAS, budget caps, brand safety constraints, inventory constraints. From monthly reviews to continuous monitoring. The agent executes thousands of changes per day. The human reviews the outcome patterns weekly and adjusts the objective function monthly. From agency-managed to brand-owned with agent support. The brand owns the data, the objective function, and the guardrails. The agent executes. The agency advises on strategy and objective function design. Transparency is the prerequisite. The agent must log every decision, the signal that triggered it, the expected outcome, and the actual outcome. The human team audits the log. The system learns from the audit. CommerceIQ's CEO Guru Hariharan frames it: "Retail is moving faster than human teams can keep up with. AI becomes truly valuable when it can understand the why and take immediate action. That is the shift to Agentic Commerce." Sources Scope3, How AI agents work in media buying and programmatic , August 2025. Scope3, What Is Agent-to-Agent Media Buying? , February 2026. measurement.title: Measurement, Inflexion
measurement.body_text: Measurement, Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Measurement Share of answer. Share of shelf. Not just clicks. How we define the only two headline numbers that matter in an AI-mediated buying journey, and what sits underneath them. Read the methodology 68% Searches end without a click Similarweb, 2025 82% Citations from earned media Muck Rack, 2025 41% GEO visibility lift Princeton / GEO KDD 2024 15.9% AI referral conversion Seer Interactive, 2025 The methodology Same questions. Same models. Comparable answers. Measurement that changes the questions every quarter is not measurement, it's a mood ring. Our methodology is fixed, auditable, and built to be re-run by anyone. 01 Fixed prompt set. We build a set of buyer questions specific to your category, covering the range from broad category questions through to comparison and purchase-intent queries. The set is fixed and published to you at the start. Changing the questions changes the number, so we don't change them without re-baselining. 02 Cross-model testing. We run the same prompt set across the models your buyers actually use. Their outputs can differ substantially. A brand can be well cited in one and absent from another. We test across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and category-relevant vertical models. 03 Source mapping. When a model names a brand, we trace what it drew from: owned content, earned media, review platforms, forums and structured data. That tells you which sources carry authority in your category. The prompt set is re-run on a fixed monthly schedule. Every run is date-stamped, model-versioned, and stored so you can compare apples to apples across quarters. What we measure Four signals. One composite picture. Headline share of answer is the composite. Each component tells you something different about how you're being surfaced, cited, and positioned. 01 Share of answer. The proportion of prompts in which your brand appears in the model output. This is the headline metric. It tells you whether you're visible at all. The baseline is always zero until you measure it. 02 Position within the answer. Being mentioned in passing and being named as the recommendation are fundamentally different outcomes. We track where in the output the brand appears: first recommendation, middle of a list or passing reference. 03 Citation velocity. How quickly new earned media and owned content are reflected in model outputs. Some brands take weeks for a press release to appear in citations. Others are reflected within days. Velocity is a leading indicator of source authority. 04 Sentiment & framing. Whether the model presents your brand neutrally, favourably or with caveats. Models do not express opinions, but their wording can frame a brand differently. A brand described as "a leading provider" competes differently from one described as "also offers." Competitive intelligence Your share means nothing without the market. Share of answer is a relative number. Knowing yours without knowing your competitors' is like knowing your position on a map without knowing where anyone else is standing. 01 Share of voice (SOV). Each competitor's share of the total brand citations across the prompt set. Who owns the answer today, who is gaining, and who is being displaced. This is the competitive baseline that most brands cannot produce because they aren't running the same prompt set against their competitors. 02 Gap analysis. We show where competitors appear and you do not, by question, model and source type. The gaps indicate what to build, earn or fix. 03 Benchmarking. How your category's discovery landscape changes over time. We track the average number of brands cited per prompt, the stability of citations across runs, and which source types are gaining or losing weight in model outputs. The measurement framework From raw data to running decisions. Measurement is useless without a framework that turns it into action. Here is how the data flows from collection through to the decisions it informs. 01 Collect Fixed prompt set run across models on a fixed schedule. Raw outputs stored, versioned, auditable. 02 Score Each brand's presence scored by occurrence, position, source type, and sentiment. Weighted by model share of use. 03 Surface Gaps surfaced by question, model, and competitor. No dashboard that hides the bad news behind averages. 04 Prioritise Gaps triaged by winability and commercial impact. The question with the highest combined score gets the work. 05 Track Month-over-month change in share of answer and share of shelf. If the number isn't moving, we change what we're doing. This is the same framework we apply to every engagement. It means the work is comparable across clients and across time. Honest limitations What this number does not tell you. digital-pr.body_text: Digital PR for AEO | Earn the Citations AI Trusts Most | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us IV. Digital PR for AEO 84% of AI citations come from earned media. Your website is 5–10% of the picture. AI models trust what others say about you more than what you say about yourself. Digital PR for AEO earns coverage in the sources models already cite: mapped, weighted, and measured against a fixed baseline. Map your citation sources → See the evidence 84% AI citations from earned media Muck Rack, May 2026 0.3% Paid/advertorial citations Muck Rack, 25M links 239% Median visibility lift Stacker x Scrunch, 2026 3× Mentions > backlinks for citations Ahrefs, 75K brands, 2025 The evidence Three studies. One conclusion. Independent research from Muck Rack, Stacker/Scrunch, and Ahrefs reports similar findings: AI engines trust earned media over owned content by a wide margin. The cited studies cover more than 1M citations, five LLMs and 75,000 brands. What AI Engines Actually Cite: Source Type Distribution Horizontal bar chart comparing citation share across source types. Earned media dominates at 84%; owned content and paid sources account for smaller shares. Source: Muck Rack "What Is AI Reading?" May 2026, 25M+ citations across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini. Stacker/Scrunch controlled study across 5 LLMs, 2026. University of Toronto peer-reviewed study, EDBT/ICDT 2026. Citation Lift: Brand Distribution vs Earned Media Distribution Slopegraph showing identical content distributed two ways: through brand-owned channels vs through third-party news outlets. Earned distribution lifts citation rate by 239% median, 325% at best. Source: Stacker x Scrunch controlled study, 2026. Five LLMs tested: ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Copilot. Identical content, different distribution channels. The pattern is consistent across every major study: 84% of AI citations are earned media Muck Rack, 25M+ citations across 17 industries 0.3% paid content in citations Muck Rack, pay-to-play barely registers 57-65% earned media for buyer queries U of Toronto peer-reviewed study, 2026 Why engines trust earned media The model has a credibility problem. Earned media is one signal that can help address it. When an AI engine decides which brand to recommend, every brand's own website says the same thing: "we are excellent." Self-published content may provide less independent corroboration. Editorial coverage carries something brands cannot manufacture: an independent party chose to write about you. That signal maps directly to how retrieval systems and training corpora weight sources. 01 Trust calibration. Models weight editorial sources as corroboration and promotional domains as claims. A mention in a trade publication with no byline link still reinforces entity recognition more than a perfectly improved product page. The model may use signals associated with the source and its content, not only the URL. 02 Entity reinforcement. Consistent third-party descriptions of what your company does build the entity graph the model relies on. Every mention that correctly names your product category, use case, and differentiators feeds the same entity signal. Conflicting descriptions confuse the model and reduce citation probability. 03 Citation velocity. How quickly new earned media appears in model outputs is a leading indicator of source authority. Brands whose coverage is reflected within days have stronger entity signals than brands whose coverage takes weeks to surface, if it surfaces at all. 04 The 2% rule. Only 2% of journalists on standard PR pitching lists overlap with the outlets AI models actually cite. Traditional PR targets the wrong people. Citation-weighted PR starts from the model's source map, not a media database subscription. The remaining contacts may be less relevant to citation-focused outreach. The source map Every category has a different citation graph. We map which outlets, forums, research papers, and data sets carry weight with AI models for your specific market. The source map is the targeting list for every piece of outreach, and it is built from the model's own citation data, not from a media database. Citation Source Distribution by AI Engine Grouped bar chart showing how each AI engine weights different source types. Claude favours earned media at 65%; Gemini draws more from owned content. PR strategy shifts by target engine. Source: Chen, Wang, Chen, Koudas, U of Toronto, EDBT/ICDT 2026. 300 consumer-electronics queries across all intent types. Earned includes journalism, academic, government/NGO, encyclopedic, social, third-party corporate. Phase 1 Source mapping We run your priority buyer prompts across 6 models and record every source cited: every domain, every outlet, every forum. The result is a ranked list of publications that carry weight in your category. This is your targeting list. Phase 2 Entity building Wikipedia, Crunchbase, G2, industry directories, analyst listings: the sources models use to answer "who is company X." We audit every reference source, fix inconsistencies, and build a complete entity footprint before scaling outreach. Phase 3 Earned coverage We target the specific outlets models cite most in your category, not the outlets in a generic media database. A mention in a specialist trade publication that AI cites more often may be more relevant than several generic mentions from a syndicated wire. Phase 4 Community presence Reddit, Quora, YouTube, Stack Exchange, niche forums: community content is a growing share of AI citations. We help develop a presence in the platforms your category's buyers use, by contributing useful answers where appropriate. How we measure Share of citation, tracked back to specific coverage. PR without measurement is activity. We run the same buyer prompts across 6 models every month and compare changes in citation volume with specific placements. 01 Baseline 30-50 buyer prompts across 6 models. Your Share of Citation measured against competitors. Source map built from live citation data. 02 Deploy Citation-weighted outreach against the source map. Entity building completed. Community presence launched. 03 Track Monthly re-run of the same prompt set. Every shift attributed to a specific placement. Sentiment and position recorded per citation. 04 Refine Source map refreshed quarterly. Outlets that do not contribute to the measured result are reviewed and may be dropped. New targets added based on model drift. Measurement in practice Baseline. Deploy. Track. Refine. The effect of earned media on AI citation cannot be measured in real time. Models re-crawl on their own schedules, and a mention published today may take weeks to appear in answers. We set expectations at month three and track from there. The shift is measured by running the same prompt set across six models every month and comparing citation volume changes with specific placements. Single placements rarely move the number alone. The effect compounds across consistent coverage in the outlets the model trusts. Earning coverage there is not a quick fix. The outlets AI models cite form a relatively narrow set, and existing traditional PR contacts rarely translate. We are honest about that from the start. Map your citation sources → See which sources AI trusts in your category. A structured citation audit across 6 models. You keep the source map either way. arguments.text: The evidence Three studies. One conclusion. Independent research from Muck Rack, Stacker/Scrunch, and Ahrefs reports similar findings: AI engines trust earned media over owned content by a wide margin. The cited studies cover more than 1M citations, five LLMs and 75,000 brands. What AI Engines Actually Cite: Source Type Distribution Horizontal bar chart comparing citation share across source types. Earned media dominates at 84%; owned content and paid sources account for smaller shares. Source: Muck Rack "What Is AI Reading?" May 2026, 25M+ citations across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini. Stacker/Scrunch controlled study across 5 LLMs, 2026. University of Toronto peer-reviewed study, EDBT/ICDT 2026. Citation Lift: Brand Distribution vs Earned Media Distribution Slopegraph showing identical content distributed two ways: through brand-owned channels vs through third-party news outlets. Earned distribution lifts citation rate by 239% median, 325% at best. Source: Stacker x Scrunch controlled study, 2026. Five LLMs tested: ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Copilot. Identical content, different distribution channels. The pattern is consistent across every major study: 84% of AI citations are earned media Muck Rack, 25M+ citations across 17 industries 0.3% paid content in citations Muck Rack, pay-to-play barely registers 57-65% earned media for buyer queries U of Toronto peer-reviewed study, 2026

Why engines trust earned media The model has a credibility problem. Earned media is one signal that can help address it. When an AI engine decides which brand to recommend, every brand's own website says the same thing: "we are excellent." Self-published content may provide less independent corroboration. Editorial coverage carries something brands cannot manufacture: an independent party chose to write about you. That signal maps directly to how retrieval systems and training corpora weight sources. 01 Trust calibration. Models weight editorial sources as corroboration and promotional domains as claims. A mention in a trade publication with no byline link still reinforces entity recognition more than a perfectly improved product page. The model may use signals associated with the source and its content, not only the URL. 02 Entity reinforcement. Consistent third-party descriptions of what your company does build the entity graph the model relies on. Every mention that correctly names your product category, use case, and differentiators feeds the same entity signal. Conflicting descriptions confuse the model and reduce citation probability. 03 Citation velocity. How quickly new earned media appears in model outputs is a leading indicator of source authority. Brands whose coverage is reflected within days have stronger entity signals than brands whose coverage takes weeks to surface, if it surfaces at all. 04 The 2% rule. Only 2% of journalists on standard PR pitching lists overlap with the outlets AI models actually cite. Traditional PR targets the wrong people. Citation-weighted PR starts from the model's source map, not a media database subscription. The remaining contacts may be less relevant to citation-focused outreach.

The source map Every category has a different citation graph. We map which outlets, forums, research papers, and data sets carry weight with AI models for your specific market. The source map is the targeting list for every piece of outreach, and it is built from the model's own citation data, not from a media database. Citation Source Distribution by AI Engine Grouped bar chart showing how each AI engine weights different source types. Claude favours earned media at 65%; Gemini draws more from owned content. PR strategy shifts by target engine. Source: Chen, Wang, Chen, Koudas, U of Toronto, EDBT/ICDT 2026. 300 consumer-electronics queries across all intent types. Earned includes journalism, academic, government/NGO, encyclopedic, social, third-party corporate. Phase 1 Source mapping We run your priority buyer prompts across 6 models and record every source cited: every domain, every outlet, every forum. The result is a ranked list of publications that carry weight in your category. This is your targeting list. Phase 2 Entity building Wikipedia, Crunchbase, G2, industry directories, analyst listings: the sources models use to answer "who is company X." We audit every reference source, fix inconsistencies, and build a complete entity footprint before scaling outreach. Phase 3 Earned coverage We target the specific outlets models cite most in your category, not the outlets in a generic media database. A mention in a specialist trade publication that AI cites more often may be more relevant than several generic mentions from a syndicated wire. Phase 4 Community presence Reddit, Quora, YouTube, Stack Exchange, niche forums: community content is a growing share of AI citations. We help develop a presence in the platforms your category's buyers use, by contributing useful answers where appropriate.

How we measure Share of citation, tracked back to specific coverage. PR without measurement is activity. We run the same buyer prompts across 6 models every month and compare changes in citation volume with specific placements. 01 Baseline 30-50 buyer prompts across 6 models. Your Share of Citation measured against competitors. Source map built from live citation data. 02 Deploy Citation-weighted outreach against the source map. Entity building completed. Community presence launched. 03 Track Monthly re-run of the same prompt set. Every shift attributed to a specific placement. Sentiment and position recorded per citation. 04 Refine Source map refreshed quarterly. Outlets that do not contribute to the measured result are reviewed and may be dropped. New targets added based on model drift.

amazon.title: Amazon, Shelf Strategy, Sponsored Ads & DSP | Inflexion
amazon.body_text: Amazon, Shelf Strategy, Sponsored Ads & DSP | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Amazon Amazon is not a media channel. It is a product algorithm. We run Sponsored Products, Brands, Display and DSP as one campaign system rather than four separate products. Amazon rewards product data completeness, conversion history and inventory depth alongside the bid. We improve all four, not just the bid. Audit your Amazon shelf → The signals that matter 60% Amazon share of retail media eMarketer, 2026 71% Units from organic Jungle Scout, 2025 4.4× Organic vs paid ROAS Marketplace Pulse, 2025 2.1M Amazon sellers (2026) Marketplace Pulse The signals What the algorithm reads: and what most setups miss. Amazon's A9 algorithm ranks products, not ads. Sponsored placements are layered on top of the organic rank, not independent of it. The signals are documented from published sources and empirical testing. 01 Product data completeness. Titles, bullet points, images, A+ content, attributes, backend search terms. The algorithm reads this before it reads the bid. Incomplete product data is the most common constraint we find. Every missing attribute is a signal gap that paid spend cannot close. 02 Review velocity and sentiment. How quickly reviews accumulate and what they say. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. A product with 500 old reviews can be outperformed by a product with 50 recent positive ones. Velocity is the signal that most brands under-invest in. 03 Conversion rate by traffic source. We track organic, sponsored and external conversion separately. A blended number hides whether the problem is product or placement. A high-spend product with low conversion may need page work, not a higher bid. 04 Price and promotion competitiveness. Relative to the alternatives shown on the same search results page. We benchmark pricing, coupon depth, and deal timing against category competitors. The algorithm rewards the combination that converts, not the lowest price alone. 05 Inventory depth and fulfilment. Stock-outs, shipping speed, and fulfilment method all feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is improved. FBA vs FBA is increasingly a ranking signal, not just a logistics choice. 06 Paid position vs organic position. We separate the two in every report. If position improves but conversion does not follow, we flag it rather than present it as success. Share of shelf is meaningless without the paid/organic split. The ad products Four surfaces. One campaign system. Amazon offers four ad products, but they are only effective when planned and reported as one system. The bid on one product affects the rank of another. We structure them as a single campaign with shared objectives, not four separate budgets. Sponsored Products The foundation of every Amazon programme. Keyword-targeted ads that appear in search results and product detail pages. We manage them against organic rank, not just ACOS. The goal is to earn the organic position through paid support, not replace organic revenue with paid spend. Sponsored Brands Brand awareness at the top of the funnel. Customisable headline ads featuring your logo, tagline, and multiple products. Measured against category share of voice, not just click-through. The attribution window is longer than Sponsored Products and we track it separately. Sponsored Display Remarketing and audience targeting. Display ads that follow shoppers across Amazon and off-platform. We use them for audience retargeting, cross-sell, and competitor conquest. The data feeds back into the product-level signal improvement loop. Amazon DSP Programmatic buying at scale. Amazon's demand-side platform for buying display, video, and audio ads on and off Amazon. We use it to drive traffic into the algorithm, feed first-party data signals, and retarget across the post-purchase journey. Rufus and AI Amazon's conversational assistant changes the discovery path. Amazon Rufus now reaches 250 million monthly users. Shoppers ask product questions in natural language, and the assistant generates answers that draw from Amazon's catalogue, review data, community Q&A and sponsored prompts. The sponsored unit inside a Rufus conversation is a different product from a Sponsored Products search placement. 01 Sponsored Products Prompts. Keyword-targeted ads that appear as product recommendations within Rufus conversations. Billable per click. Structured as intent-based placements, not search-result slots. 02 Sponsored Brands Prompts. Brand-level recommendations within the conversational interface. Category discovery prompts that answer "what should I look for" type questions, guiding the shopper toward a specific brand's range. 03 Product data as the interface. Rufus reads the same catalogue data that A9 uses. If a product's attributes, review content and inventory signals are strong, Rufus is more likely to recommend it. Product data completeness affects both the search algorithm and the conversational recommendation. Find out what your Amazon shelf actually looks like. A full signal audit across your catalogue. Paid and organic separated. You keep the baseline either way. Audit your Amazon shelf → Amazon advertising as a connected system. ai-visibility-analytics.body_text: AI Visibility Analytics | Track Brand Performance in LLMs | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us AI Visibility Analytics Measure your brand's AI search performance. Track how your brand appears across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude, Amazon Rufus and more. Share of voice, citation sources, competitor positioning: everything you need to act. See how we measure → Competitive intelligence 11% Domain overlap between GPT & Perplexity Source: Similarweb, 2026 AI Brand Visibility Index 30% Brand visibility consistency Source: AirOps, 2026 State of AI Search 5x AI referral conversion vs organic Source: Seer Interactive, 2025 42.8% AI search traffic growth YoY Source: Similarweb, 2026 The problem You cannot improve what you do not measure. Most brands have no baseline for their AI visibility. They know what their Google rankings look like. They know their Amazon share of voice. But they have no picture of how often they appear in AI-generated answers, across which models, in response to which buyer questions, and against which competitors. 30% of brands stay visible across consecutive AI sessions. The other 70% are not consistently visible across sessions. A baseline is the only way to tell if you are gaining or losing ground. Source: AirOps, 2026 State of AI Search The gap between search and answer is real: brands ranking first on Google are entirely absent from the AI answer to the same query. We have measured it. Without measurement, the work is guesswork. The analytics provide the baseline for the work that follows. What we track Multi-model, multi-dimension. We run targeted prompts daily across the models your buyers actually use. The result is a dataset that tells you where you stand, who you are competing against, and what is driving the answers, with visibility into the prompts, responses and citation sources included in the dataset. 8+ AI models tracked daily ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Rufus & more 1000s Targeted prompts per day Buyer-intent query sets across categories 5 Citation source categories Earned, owned, review, social, forum 100% Transparent methodology Every prompt, response & citation logged Brand Visibility Profile Across Models Radar chart comparing your brand's citation rate, mention rate, sentiment, position, and consistency across 6 major AI platforms. Each axis = one metric; larger area = stronger overall presence. Mock data, replace with live API data. Axes: Citation Rate, Mention Rate, Sentiment Score, Avg. Position, Consistency, Prominence. Weekly Visibility Trend by Model Sparklines show 12-week share-of-voice trend per model. Identical y-axis scale enables direct comparison. Min/max markers flag volatility. ChatGPT Min: 12% Max: 28% Perplexity Min: 8% Max: 22% Gemini Min: 5% Max: 18% Claude Min: 3% Max: 15% Amazon Rufus Min: 1% Max: 9% Copilot Min: 2% Max: 11% Multi-model tracking Monitor brand presence across every major AI platform. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google Gemini, Claude, Amazon Rufus, Walmart Sparky, Grok, and more. Models disagree more than expected; a brand well-cited in Claude can be entirely absent from GPT. The reported 11% domain overlap illustrates the difference. We track multiple platforms to show how results vary between them. Prompt-level analysis See the exact prompts and responses behind every mention. Understand not just how often you appear, but how you are positioned versus competitors across different buyer scenarios: from broad awareness queries like "best [category]" to comparison queries like "[brand] vs [brand]" and purchase-intent questions. Every response is captured and categorised. Citation intelligence Discover which sources influence AI recommendations in your category. Reddit, Wikipedia, Quora, YouTube, analyst reports, niche forums: the source map shows where competitors earn citations that you do not, informing your content and PR strategies. One cited study reports that 82% of AI citations came from earned media, not owned content. We map where yours land. Sentiment analysis Monitor how AI platforms position your brand versus competitors. Track sentiment patterns across different models and topics. Are you recommended positively? Mentioned neutrally? Absent? The sentiment picture tells you whether your brand narrative is landing where it matters, and which competitors are more positively positioned in AI answers. Competitive intelligence Know where you stand against every competitor. Competitive Share of Voice: 3-Month Shift Slopegraph comparing your brand's AI SoV vs top 4 competitors across 6 models. Lines slope up = gaining ground; down = losing. Direct labels replace legend. Mock data, replace with live API data. Each line = one brand. Dots = current month; labels show 3-month delta. SOV Share of voice across every model. See how frequently you appear versus competitors across different AI platforms and product categories. Track which specific models and topics your competitors dominate. A brand with 40% share on ChatGPT may have 0% on Perplexity. The 11% domain overlap between the two makes SOV per-model the only meaningful metric. Gap Competitive citation gap analysis. Identify exactly where you are missing citations compared to each competitor. See every source they draw from that you do not, and the ones that neither of you owns yet. These gaps can help prioritise content and PR opportunities, ranked by citation frequency across models. Benchmark Category performance benchmarking. Compare your AI visibility against industry benchmarks. Understand whether your category is under-improved (most are) and where the quick wins sit. Only 30% of brands maintain consistent visibility across sessions. That may provide an advantage. If not, the gap can still be tracked over time. The evidence What the data actually says. Research from Princeton, Similarweb, Ahrefs and Muck Rack is cited below, with sources and dates shown for each figure. Where AI Citations Come From: Source Type Distribution Radial area chart showing citation source composition across 75,000 brands. Earned media dominates at 82%; owned content only 12%. Segment angles = share; radius = trust score (citation velocity × authority). Mock data, replace with live API data. Source: Ahrefs 75K-brand study 2025; Muck Rack 2025. "How consistent is AI brand visibility?" Only 30% of brands stay visible across consecutive AI sessions AirOps, 2026 State of AI Search "Do ChatGPT and Perplexity cite the same sources?" Only 11% domain overlap; they draw from fundamentally different content Similarweb, 2026 Generative AI Brand Visibility Index "How do AI visitors convert?" AI-referred visitors convert at 15.9%; 5x higher than the 3% organic average Seer Interactive, June 2025 "What drives AI visibility?" Brand mentions correlate 3x stronger than backlinks for AI citations Ahrefs, 75,000-brand study, 2025 "Where do AI citations come from?" 82% of AI citations are earned media, not owned content Muck Rack, December 2025 "Does SEO position matter for AI?" 83% of AI citations come from outside the organic top 10 ConvertMate, 2026 Visibility vs attribution Share of answer tells you what AI says. It does not tell you what sold. Share of answer is a leading indicator. It measures whether your brand appears in AI-generated answers, at what position, and in what context. It does not measure whether that appearance drove revenue. Those are two different measurement problems. We track both. AI Visibility Analytics gives you the share-of-answer baseline, run monthly against a fixed prompt set. Measurement ties those signals to commercial outcomes where the data allows. The methodologies are separate, transparent and published. See the measurement methodology → See what AI actually says about your brand. A structured analytics baseline across the AI platforms that matter. You keep the data; we help you act on it. Get your baseline → AI visibility measured, not assumed. aeo-rankings-to-citations.title: AEO: the shift from keyword rankings to citation tracking | Inflexion
aeo-rankings-to-citations.body_text: AEO: the shift from keyword rankings to citation tracking | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media & the Algorithmic Shelf Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us AI Discovery / AEO AEO: the shift from keyword rankings to citation tracking Search is no longer about ranking for keywords. It is about being cited in AI answers. Here is how the measurement model is changing. 19 September 2026 · 10 min read · Inflexion journal On this page 01 / The old model 02 / The new model 03 / What measurement looks like now 04 / Different engines, different signals 05 / What this means for your strategy For two decades, the SEO playbook was stable. Rank for keywords. Drive traffic. Convert visitors. The metric that mattered was position one through ten. That model is breaking. Not because SEO stopped working. Because the surface where discovery happens has shifted. Semrush projects that LLM referral traffic will overtake traditional Google search by the end of 2027. In the past three months alone, LLM referrals grew 800 percent year over year. Google AI Overviews now appear on billions of searches monthly, covering at least 13 percent of all SERPs. The surface has changed. The measurement has not caught up. 01. The old model was built for clicks. The new model is built for citations. The old question: where do we rank for this keyword? The new question: does the model cite us when someone asks this question? They are not the same. A page ranking position three for a keyword may be absent from the AI answer to the same query. We have measured this gap across dozens of categories. It is larger than most marketing teams realise. AI Overviews and chatbots do not simply read the top ten results. They retrieve from a wider index, weight authority differently, and prefer content structured for direct extraction. The metric that matters is not position. It is share of answer. How often does your brand appear in the generated response? At what position within the answer? With what sentiment? Ranking is a proxy for visibility. Citation is visibility itself. 02. The signals have changed. The playbook has not caught up. Traditional SEO measures keyword density, backlink volume, page speed, and technical crawlability. AEO uses different signals. Authority now means how often other trusted sources cite you. Backlinks still matter. But unlinked brand mentions across Reddit, Wikipedia, YouTube, industry forums, and news outlets now carry weight. LLMs read the text around your brand name. They do not require a hyperlink to register the association. Relevance means whether your content directly answers the question being asked. Keyword density matters less than factual clarity. A clear, direct answer in the first paragraph of a page outweighs keyword-stuffed content that buries the answer. Clarity means whether the model can parse your content. Structure matters. Schema markup, FAQ format, clear headings, and extractable answers help the model retrieve and cite you. Pages with quotes or statistics have been shown to have 30 to 40 percent higher visibility in AI answers. Freshness means how recent your content is. LLMs have a clear preference for recent content. Content audits are non-negotiable. Update statistics, screenshots, and examples. Remove references to outdated tools. Add new sections covering recent developments. The old playbook: keyword density, backlink volume, page speed. The new playbook: authority mentions, direct answers, extractable structure, content freshness. 03. Measurement has moved from rankings to share of answer. You cannot improve what you do not measure. The old dashboard showed keyword rankings, organic traffic, and click-through rate. The new dashboard needs different metrics. Share of answer: the proportion of a defined buyer prompt set, across a defined set of models, in which your brand appears in the generated answer. Position within the answer is recorded. Being named as the first recommendation is different from being mentioned in a list of three. Citation sources: when a model names a competitor, trace what it drew from. Independent reviews, comparison tables, analyst reports, forum discussions. The source map tells you exactly where to build credibility. Sentiment and framing: is your brand recommended positively, mentioned neutrally, or described with caveats? Models do not express opinions, but their wording frames brands differently. A brand described as "a leading provider" competes differently from one described as "also offers." Cross-model consistency: models disagree. A brand well-cited in Claude can be absent from GPT. The 11 percent domain overlap between ChatGPT and Perplexity proves it. You need visibility across the models your buyers actually use. The prompt set is fixed and published. The number means something because the questions did not change. 04. Different engines, different signals. One strategy does not transfer. ChatGPT favors credible, authoritative sources with clear entity signals. Comparison content has a 95 percent citation rate. Documentation and resources hit 86 percent. Google Gemini pulls heavily from pages that already perform well organically, typically within the top 20 results. Blog content performs particularly well in AI Overviews at 42 percent citation rate. Perplexity cites well-researched, comprehensive content that combines multiple perspectives. Academic sources and data-driven content perform well. Blog posts and informative articles hit 80 percent citation rate. Copilot favors content that clearly states what a product or service does, includes pricing or comparison information, and has strong brand signals. The strategy shifts by target engine. A single approach does not transfer. You need to know which engines your buyers use and match their specific retrieval logic. 05. What this means for your strategy. The shift is not optional. On Marketing's October 2025 survey found that 37 percent of marketing teams are already actively optimising for AI search. Another 30 percent are exploring it. Eighty percent plan to have AI search strategies in place within a year. The teams that start tracking now will have the baseline when the market catches up. The teams that wait will be measuring from zero. Start with a pilot. Map 5 to 10 high-priority buyer questions. Test across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews. Record where you appear, where competitors appear, and where nobody does. That baseline document is yours to keep. Then build the system: prompt mapping, citation tracking, source authority mapping, content built for citation. Track monthly against the fixed prompt set. The number means something because the questions did not change. AEO does not replace SEO. Strong SEO fuels AEO. AI systems favour content from trusted domains with strong organic rankings. But the measurement model has shifted. The teams that understand the new metrics will make better decisions. The teams that keep reporting keyword rankings will be reporting on a surface that matters less every quarter. ecommerce-whitepaper.body_text: The Future of Ecommerce Shopping in an AI World | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Retail Media Beauty Report Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Inflexion Whitepaper · September 2026 The Future of Ecommerce Shopping in an AI World How AI is changing discovery, advertising, retail media, consideration and the economics of ecommerce. Contents What this whitepaper covers Introduction: The interface is changing 07 Retail media after the search result 01 The shopper has changed 08 From buying impressions to influencing decisions 02 The consideration set becomes the battleground 09 Measurement breaks 03 From search advertising to AI-mediated advertising 10 Category changes everything 04 Product data becomes media infrastructure 11 What marketers need to change 05 Brand before the prompt 12 The emerging AI commerce system 06 The validation economy Introduction The interface is changing. The way people shop online is being redesigned in real time, and the people doing the redesigning are not retailers. They are AI laboratories building shopping agents that sit between the buyer and every seller on the internet. Fifty-two percent of US consumers now use AI when shopping, according to the IAB. ChatGPT passes nine hundred million weekly users. Amazon's Rufus has surpassed two hundred and fifty million monthly users. By 2028, McKinsey projects that seven hundred and fifty billion dollars in US revenue will funnel through AI-powered search. AI already mediates commerce. What is less understood is how comprehensively the shift rewires every layer of the ecommerce system: discovery, advertising, product data, brand equity, validation, retail media, measurement and the economics of categories. The search box is becoming an answer. The product page is becoming a data feed. The checkout is becoming an API. This whitepaper examines the evidence already available and draws the implications for brands, retailers and platforms. It does not predict. It reports what is happening, what the data shows, and what that means for anyone selling goods through digital commerce. AI already mediates commerce. Inflexion 52% Of US consumers now use AI when shopping IAB, 2025 900M+ ChatGPT weekly active users OpenAI, 2026 $750B US revenue projected through AI-powered search by 2028 McKinsey 01 The shopper has changed The shopper has changed. The data is unequivocal. The most striking single data point is from Adobe: AI-referred traffic to US retail sites grew 1,324% since October 2024. In March 2026 alone, AI traffic to US retail sites was up 269% year on year. By May 2026, it was still growing at 138% YoY. This is not a niche behaviour. Shopify reports that AI traffic to its merchants' stores is up seven times and AI-attributed orders up eleven times since January 2025. Orders from AI searches rose nearly thirteen times in early 2026. The early narrative that AI traffic converts poorly has reversed: Adobe's 2026 data shows AI traffic now converts comparably to non-AI traffic. The shopper who arrives via AI is not a lower-quality lead. The shopper who arrives via AI is simply a shopper. The technology that brought them has become a primary discovery mechanism. During Cyber Week 2025, Salesforce found that 20% of global orders were influenced by AI agents. One in five purchases already involved an AI somewhere in the decision chain. That number will not shrink. 1,324% Growth in AI-referred traffic to US retail sites since Oct 2024 Adobe, 2026 269% YoY increase in AI traffic to US retail sites, March 2026 Adobe 20% Of global orders influenced by AI agents during Cyber Week 2025 Salesforce The early narrative that AI traffic converts poorly has reversed. AI traffic now converts comparably to non-AI traffic. Adobe, 2026 The Changing Shopping Journey Shopper need → AI answer engine → Product recommendation → Human validation → Purchase The linear search-funnel model is being replaced by a recommendation-validation-purchase loop mediated by AI at every stage. 7x AI traffic to Shopify stores has increased sevenfold since January 2025. AI-attributed orders rose eleven times in the same period. Orders from AI searches rose nearly thirteen times in early 2026. Shopify, 2026 02 The consideration set The consideration set becomes the battleground. Search advertising worked because a shopper who typed a query was actively considering a set of options and the advertiser could insert into that set. AI answers change this. When a user asks ChatGPT or Google's AI Mode for a product recommendation, the answer is a curated list of three to five options. The consideration set is determined by the model, not by the shopper's own browsing. This has a measurable effect. Similarweb data from 2026 shows that Google AI Mode generates referral traffic on only 1.6% to 2.5% of queries, compared with the 17% to 19% referral rate from traditional Google search. The zero-click rate has risen to 64.82% in 2026, up from roughly 50% in 2019. More shoppers get the answer without ever visiting a site. Being left out of the AI answer is not the same as ranking low on a search results page. It is invisibility. McKinsey estimates brands may see 20% to 50% traffic decline from traditional search as AI-mediated discovery expands. The consideration set is not being rearranged. It is being replaced. Being left out of the AI answer is not the same as ranking low on a search results page. It is invisibility. Inflexion 1.6-2.5% AI Mode referral rate vs 17-19% for traditional Google search Similarweb, 2026 64.82% Zero-click search rate in 2026, up from ~50% in 2019 Similarweb 20-50% Potential traffic decline from traditional search for brands McKinsey 17-19% Traditional Google search sends referral traffic to websites on 17-19% of queries. Google AI Mode generates referrals on just 1.6-2.5% of queries. The gap represents the collapse of the traditional search traffic model. Similarweb, 2026 The consideration set is not being rearranged. It is being replaced. Inflexion 03 Advertising From search advertising to AI-mediated advertising. For twenty years, search advertising was simple: the shopper typed a keyword and the advertiser bought the keyword. AI answers do not surface keyword-matched ads in any recognisable form. They generate natural language responses that incorporate product recommendations, and increasingly, those recommendations can be sponsored. Google is testing new ad formats integrated directly into AI Mode responses, announced May 2026. Google AI Max for Shopping, launched April 2026, offers text customisation, flexible user engagement and optimal format selection. Amazon's Rufus exited beta for Sponsored Products and Brands Prompts in March 2026, operating on a billable CPC model within the conversational interface. These are not experiments. These are the foundations of a new advertising model in which the ad unit is not a slot on a page but a recommendation in a conversation. The advertiser no longer buys a keyword. They buy inclusion in a generated answer. 2026 The year every major platform launched or tested native AI-native advertising: Google Ads in AI Mode (May), Google AI Max for Shopping (April), and Amazon Rufus Sponsored Products Prompts exiting beta (March). The ad unit is becoming the recommendation. Google, Amazon, 2026 The advertiser no longer buys a keyword. They buy inclusion in a generated answer. Inflexion The Shift in Advertising Placement Search keyword → Sponsored listing → Click & conversion — becomes — Shopper prompt → AI-generated answer → Sponsored recommendation → Attributed purchase The ad moves from a separate slot on a results page to a recommendation embedded within the AI's natural language answer. Mar 2026 Amazon Rufus Sponsored Products/Brands Prompts exited beta, billable CPC Amazon Apr 2026 Google AI Max for Shopping launched with text customisation and FUE Google May 2026 Google announced testing new ad formats integrated into AI Mode Google 04 Product data Product data becomes media infrastructure. An AI shopping agent does not read a website. It reads structured data: product feeds, schema markup, merchant centre listings, API responses. If a product's attributes are not machine-readable, the product does not exist in the AI's consideration universe. Google's Shopping Graph contains over sixty billion product listings. When Gemini searches for a product, it queries that graph, not the open web. Amazon Rufus draws from Amazon's own catalogue. OpenAI's ACP (launched September 2025) connects ChatGPT directly to merchant product feeds. The infrastructure of commerce is becoming the data feed, not the product page. This is why Google launched the Universal Commerce Protocol in January 2026, with checkout rolling out across the US, Canada, Australia and the UK. UCP is a standardised checkout API that allows any AI agent to complete a purchase on any participating merchant's site without the shopper leaving the conversation. Amazon's Buy for Me, launched April 2025, already does this: the agent buys from a brand's own website on the shopper's behalf. If a product's attributes are not machine-readable, the product does not exist in the AI's consideration universe. Inflexion 60B+ Products in Google's Shopping Graph Google Sep 2025 OpenAI ACP launched: agentic commerce protocol connecting ChatGPT to merchant feeds OpenAI Apr 2025 Amazon Buy for Me launched: agentic purchases from brand websites Amazon The Product Data Chain Product attributes → Structured feed → Shopping Graph → AI agent query → Recommendation → Agentic checkout Data flows from product attributes through structured feeds to AI agents, bypassing the brand's own website entirely for discovery and increasingly for purchase. The infrastructure of commerce is becoming the data feed, not the product page. Inflexion 05 Brand before the prompt Brand before the prompt. An AI agent can only recommend a brand it recognises from its training data, its knowledge graph or its retrieval corpus. If a brand is not present in the sources the model trusts, it will not appear in the answer. This is not an SEO problem. This is a brand-awareness problem mediated by a language model. The implication is that brand building has become an AI visibility strategy. The brands mentioned in authoritative editorial coverage, verified retailer pages, community discussions and creator content are the brands that appear in answers. A brand that has invested in awareness, earned media and structured presence across the web is a brand the model can find. Gartner's January 2026 survey found that only 11% of US consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions entirely, while 31% are willing to let it narrow choices for household supplies. Trust in AI recommendations is still being earned. Brands that build recognition and credibility outside the AI channel bring that trust into the AI answer when the model selects them. If a brand is not present in the sources the model trusts, it will not appear in the answer. This is not an SEO problem. Inflexion 11% Of US consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions entirely. Just 31% will let it narrow choices for household supplies. The majority still want human agency in the decision. Gartner, January 2026 Brand building has become an AI visibility strategy. The brands the model can find are the brands that appear in the answer. Inflexion 06 The validation economy The validation economy: trust is the currency. The AI recommendation is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of a validation phase in which the shopper checks, compares and confirms before buying. Gartner's November-December 2025 survey found that 54% of AI shoppers had to double-check the accuracy of all information provided, and 62% said the AI-provided information was a waste of time. These numbers describe a trust gap that commerce infrastructure must close. The brands that win in this environment are those that not only appear in the AI answer but also provide the validation content the shopper needs to say yes: reviews, creator content, retailer listings, comparison data. Each validation surface is a moment where a brand can be confirmed or rejected. This creates what can be called a validation economy, in which the brands that own the best evidence across reviews, social proof, editorial coverage and retailer presence capture the conversion. Trust is not a brand attribute. It is a media asset that must be built, maintained and surfaced at the moment of doubt. 54% Of AI shoppers had to double-check accuracy of all information Gartner, Nov-Dec 2025 62% Said AI-provided shopping information was a waste of time Gartner, 2025 Trust is not a brand attribute. It is a media asset that must be built, maintained and surfaced at the moment of doubt. Inflexion 62% Of consumers who used AI for shopping found the information a waste of time. Yet 52% continue to use AI for shopping. The behaviour persists despite dissatisfaction because the alternative — traditional search — is also deteriorating. Gartner, November-December 2025 Each validation surface is a moment where a brand can be confirmed or rejected. Inflexion 07 Retail media Retail media after the search result. US retail media spend is projected to reach $71.09 billion in 2026, according to eMarketer. The growth has been driven by the logic that the retailer owns the transaction and can monetise the path to it. But if the transaction moves to an AI agent that does not land on the retailer's search results page, the economics of retail media shift. Amazon Rufus now shows Sponsored Products and Brands within the conversational AI interface. The ad unit is not a search result slot. It is a recommendation in a dialogue. Google UCP and OpenAI ACP create checkout experiences that occur outside the retailer's owned environment entirely. The retail media impression that used to happen on a product listing page now happens inside an AI conversation, and the measurement framework must follow. The retailer's control over the shopper's attention erodes as AI agents intermediate. The sponsored slot on a search results page is replaced by the sponsored mention in an AI answer. The auction moves upstream, from the search query to the training data and retrieval corpus that determine the AI's recommendation. The auction moves upstream, from the search query to the training data and retrieval corpus that determine the AI's recommendation. Inflexion $71.09B Projected US retail media ad spend in 2026 eMarketer 250M+ Monthly active users on Amazon Rufus Amazon $71B US retail media spend in 2026. The infrastructure that supported this spend — search results page ads, sponsored product slots, display on retailer sites — is being disrupted by AI agents that mediate discovery and purchase outside the retailer's owned environment. eMarketer, 2026 08 Influencing decisions From buying impressions to influencing decisions. The payment infrastructure is following the AI agent. Visa launched Intelligent Commerce Connect in April 2026, working with OpenAI ACP, Google UCP and Mastercard's Multi-Party Payments protocol. Mastercard Agent Pay, launched in 2025, is already working with Microsoft Copilot Checkout. The checkout that was once a secure page on a retailer's site is becoming an API call from an AI conversation. OpenAI's Instant Checkout, launched alongside ACP, was retired in March 2026 after the company pivoted ACP to focus on product discovery rather than full checkout. The direction of travel is clear: every major card network and AI platform is building the infrastructure for agent-initiated payments. The purchase decision is being unbundled from the purchase execution. Marketing is no longer about buying impressions that lead to a checkout page. sections.heading: The interface is changing.
sections.text: Introduction The interface is changing. The way people shop online is being redesigned in real time, and the people doing the redesigning are not retailers. They are AI laboratories building shopping agents that sit between the buyer and every seller on the internet. Fifty-two percent of US consumers now use AI when shopping, according to the IAB. ChatGPT passes nine hundred million weekly users. Amazon's Rufus has surpassed two hundred and fifty million monthly users. By 2028, McKinsey projects that seven hundred and fifty billion dollars in US revenue will funnel through AI-powered search. AI already mediates commerce. What is less understood is how comprehensively the shift rewires every layer of the ecommerce system: discovery, advertising, product data, brand equity, validation, retail media, measurement and the economics of categories. The search box is becoming an answer. The product page is becoming a data feed. The checkout is becoming an API. This whitepaper examines the evidence already available and draws the implications for brands, retailers and platforms. It does not predict. It reports what is happening, what the data shows, and what that means for anyone selling goods through digital commerce. AI already mediates commerce. sections.heading: The shopper has changed. The data is unequivocal.
sections.text: 01 The shopper has changed The shopper has changed. The data is unequivocal. The most striking single data point is from Adobe: AI-referred traffic to US retail sites grew 1,324% since October 2024. In March 2026 alone, AI traffic to US retail sites was up 269% year on year. By May 2026, it was still growing at 138% YoY. This is not a niche behaviour. Shopify reports that AI traffic to its merchants' stores is up seven times and AI-attributed orders up eleven times since January 2025. Orders from AI searches rose nearly thirteen times in early 2026. The early narrative that AI traffic converts poorly has reversed: Adobe's 2026 data shows AI traffic now converts comparably to non-AI traffic. The shopper who arrives via AI is not a lower-quality lead. The shopper who arrives via AI is simply a shopper. The technology that brought them has become a primary discovery mechanism. During Cyber Week 2025, Salesforce found that 20% of global orders were influenced by AI agents. One in five purchases already involved an AI somewhere in the decision chain. That number will not shrink. 1,324% Growth in AI-referred traffic to US retail sites since Oct 2024 Adobe, 2026 269% YoY increase in AI traffic to US retail sites, March 2026 Adobe 20% Of global orders influenced by AI agents during Cyber Week 2025 Salesforce The early narrative that AI traffic converts poorly has reversed. AI traffic now converts comparably to non-AI traffic. sections.heading: The consideration set becomes the battleground.
sections.text: 02 The consideration set The consideration set becomes the battleground. Search advertising worked because a shopper who typed a query was actively considering a set of options and the advertiser could insert into that set. AI answers change this. When a user asks ChatGPT or Google's AI Mode for a product recommendation, the answer is a curated list of three to five options. The consideration set is determined by the model, not by the shopper's own browsing. This has a measurable effect. Similarweb data from 2026 shows that Google AI Mode generates referral traffic on only 1.6% to 2.5% of queries, compared with the 17% to 19% referral rate from traditional Google search. The zero-click rate has risen to 64.82% in 2026, up from roughly 50% in 2019. More shoppers get the answer without ever visiting a site. Being left out of the AI answer is not the same as ranking low on a search results page. It is invisibility. McKinsey estimates brands may see 20% to 50% traffic decline from traditional search as AI-mediated discovery expands. The consideration set is not being rearranged. It is being replaced. Being left out of the AI answer is not the same as ranking low on a search results page. It is invisibility. Google AI Mode generates referrals on just 1.6-2.5% of queries. The gap represents the collapse of the traditional search traffic model. Similarweb, 2026

sections.heading: From search advertising to AI-mediated advertising.
sections.text: 03 Advertising From search advertising to AI-mediated advertising. For twenty years, search advertising was simple: the shopper typed a keyword and the advertiser bought the keyword. AI answers do not surface keyword-matched ads in any recognisable form. They generate natural language responses that incorporate product recommendations, and increasingly, those recommendations can be sponsored. Google is testing new ad formats integrated directly into AI Mode responses, announced May 2026. Google AI Max for Shopping, launched April 2026, offers text customisation, flexible user engagement and optimal format selection. Amazon's Rufus exited beta for Sponsored Products and Brands Prompts in March 2026, operating on a billable CPC model within the conversational interface. These are not experiments. These are the foundations of a new advertising model in which the ad unit is not a slot on a page but a recommendation in a conversation. The advertiser no longer buys a keyword. They buy inclusion in a generated answer. 2026 The year every major platform launched or tested native AI-native advertising: Google Ads in AI Mode (May), Google AI Max for Shopping (April), and Amazon Rufus Sponsored Products Prompts exiting beta (March). The ad unit is becoming the recommendation. Google, Amazon, 2026 The advertiser no longer buys a keyword. They buy inclusion in a generated answer. sections.heading: Product data becomes media infrastructure.
sections.text: 04 Product data Product data becomes media infrastructure. An AI shopping agent does not read a website. It reads structured data: product feeds, schema markup, merchant centre listings, API responses. If a product's attributes are not machine-readable, the product does not exist in the AI's consideration universe. Google's Shopping Graph contains over sixty billion product listings. When Gemini searches for a product, it queries that graph, not the open web. Amazon Rufus draws from Amazon's own catalogue. OpenAI's ACP (launched September 2025) connects ChatGPT directly to merchant product feeds. The infrastructure of commerce is becoming the data feed, not the product page. This is why Google launched the Universal Commerce Protocol in January 2026, with checkout rolling out across the US, Canada, Australia and the UK. UCP is a standardised checkout API that allows any AI agent to complete a purchase on any participating merchant's site without the shopper leaving the conversation. Amazon's Buy for Me, launched April 2025, already does this: the agent buys from a brand's own website on the shopper's behalf. If a product's attributes are not machine-readable, the product does not exist in the AI's consideration universe. sections.heading: Brand before the prompt.
sections.text: 05 Brand before the prompt Brand before the prompt. An AI agent can only recommend a brand it recognises from its training data, its knowledge graph or its retrieval corpus. If a brand is not present in the sources the model trusts, it will not appear in the answer. This is not an SEO problem. This is a brand-awareness problem mediated by a language model. The implication is that brand building has become an AI visibility strategy. The brands mentioned in authoritative editorial coverage, verified retailer pages, community discussions and creator content are the brands that appear in answers. A brand that has invested in awareness, earned media and structured presence across the web is a brand the model can find. Gartner's January 2026 survey found that only 11% of US consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions entirely, while 31% are willing to let it narrow choices for household supplies. Trust in AI recommendations is still being earned. Brands that build recognition and credibility outside the AI channel bring that trust into the AI answer when the model selects them. If a brand is not present in the sources the model trusts, it will not appear in the answer. This is not an SEO problem. sections.heading: The validation economy: trust is the currency.
sections.text: 06 The validation economy The validation economy: trust is the currency. The AI recommendation is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of a validation phase in which the shopper checks, compares and confirms before buying. Gartner's November-December 2025 survey found that 54% of AI shoppers had to double-check the accuracy of all information provided, and 62% said the AI-provided information was a waste of time. These numbers describe a trust gap that commerce infrastructure must close. The brands that win in this environment are those that not only appear in the AI answer but also provide the validation content the shopper needs to say yes: reviews, creator content, retailer listings, comparison data. Each validation surface is a moment where a brand can be confirmed or rejected. This creates what can be called a validation economy, in which the brands that own the best evidence across reviews, social proof, editorial coverage and retailer presence capture the conversion. Trust is not a brand attribute. It is a media asset that must be built, maintained and surfaced at the moment of doubt. 54% Of AI shoppers had to double-check accuracy of all information Gartner, Nov-Dec 2025 62% Said AI-provided shopping information was a waste of time Gartner, 2025 Trust is not a brand attribute. It is a media asset that must be built, maintained and surfaced at the moment of doubt. Inflexion 62% Of consumers who used AI for shopping found the information a waste of time. Yet 52% continue to use AI for shopping. The behaviour persists despite dissatisfaction because the alternative — traditional search — is also deteriorating. Gartner, November-December 2025

sections.text: 07 Retail media Retail media after the search result. US retail media spend is projected to reach $71.09 billion in 2026, according to eMarketer. The growth has been driven by the logic that the retailer owns the transaction and can monetise the path to it. But if the transaction moves to an AI agent that does not land on the retailer's search results page, the economics of retail media shift. Amazon Rufus now shows Sponsored Products and Brands within the conversational AI interface. The ad unit is not a search result slot. It is a recommendation in a dialogue. Google UCP and OpenAI ACP create checkout experiences that occur outside the retailer's owned environment entirely. The retail media impression that used to happen on a product listing page now happens inside an AI conversation, and the measurement framework must follow. The retailer's control over the shopper's attention erodes as AI agents intermediate. The sponsored slot on a search results page is replaced by the sponsored mention in an AI answer. The auction moves upstream, from the search query to the training data and retrieval corpus that determine the AI's recommendation. The auction moves upstream, from the search query to the training data and retrieval corpus that determine the AI's recommendation. The infrastructure that supported this spend — search results page ads, sponsored product slots, display on retailer sites — is being disrupted by AI agents that mediate discovery and purchase outside the retailer's owned environment. eMarketer, 2026

The direction of travel is clear: every major card network and AI platform is building the infrastructure for agent-initiated payments.
