01 The shopper has changed The shopper has changed. The data is unequivocal. The most striking single data point is from Adobe: AI-referred traffic to US retail sites grew 1,324% since October 2024. In March 2026 alone, AI traffic to US retail sites was up 269% year on year. By May 2026, it was still growing at 138% YoY. This is not a niche behaviour. Shopify reports that AI traffic to its merchants' stores is up seven times and AI-attributed orders up eleven times since January 2025. Orders from AI searches rose nearly thirteen times in early 2026. The early narrative that AI traffic converts poorly has reversed: Adobe's 2026 data shows AI traffic now converts comparably to non-AI traffic. The shopper who arrives via AI is not a lower-quality lead. The shopper who arrives via AI is simply a shopper. The technology that brought them has become a primary discovery mechanism. During Cyber Week 2025, Salesforce found that 20% of global orders were influenced by AI agents. One in five purchases already involved an AI somewhere in the decision chain. That number will not shrink. 1,324% Growth in AI-referred traffic to US retail sites since Oct 2024 Adobe, 2026 269% YoY increase in AI traffic to US retail sites, March 2026 Adobe 20% Of global orders influenced by AI agents during Cyber Week 2025 Salesforce The early narrative that AI traffic converts poorly has reversed. AI traffic now converts comparably to non-AI traffic. Adobe, 2026 The Changing Shopping Journey Shopper need → AI answer engine → Product recommendation → Human validation → Purchase The linear search-funnel model is being replaced by a recommendation-validation-purchase loop mediated by AI at every stage. 7x AI traffic to Shopify stores has increased sevenfold since January 2025. AI-attributed orders rose eleven times in the same period. Orders from AI searches rose nearly thirteen times in early 2026. Shopify, 2026

02 The consideration set The consideration set becomes the battleground. Search advertising worked because a shopper who typed a query was actively considering a set of options and the advertiser could insert into that set. AI answers change this. When a user asks ChatGPT or Google's AI Mode for a product recommendation, the answer is a curated list of three to five options. The consideration set is determined by the model, not by the shopper's own browsing. This has a measurable effect. Similarweb data from 2026 shows that Google AI Mode generates referral traffic on only 1.6% to 2.5% of queries, compared with the 17% to 19% referral rate from traditional Google search. The zero-click rate has risen to 64.82% in 2026, up from roughly 50% in 2019. More shoppers get the answer without ever visiting a site. Being left out of the AI answer is not the same as ranking low on a search results page. It is invisibility. McKinsey estimates brands may see 20% to 50% traffic decline from traditional search as AI-mediated discovery expands. The consideration set is not being rearranged. It is being replaced. Being left out of the AI answer is not the same as ranking low on a search results page. It is invisibility. Inflexion 1.6-2.5% AI Mode referral rate vs 17-19% for traditional Google search Similarweb, 2026 64.82% Zero-click search rate in 2026, up from ~50% in 2019 Similarweb 20-50% Potential traffic decline from traditional search for brands McKinsey 17-19% Traditional Google search sends referral traffic to websites on 17-19% of queries. Google AI Mode generates referrals on just 1.6-2.5% of queries. The gap represents the collapse of the traditional search traffic model. Similarweb, 2026

03 Advertising From search advertising to AI-mediated advertising. For twenty years, search advertising was simple: the shopper typed a keyword and the advertiser bought the keyword. AI answers do not surface keyword-matched ads in any recognisable form. They generate natural language responses that incorporate product recommendations, and increasingly, those recommendations can be sponsored. Google is testing new ad formats integrated directly into AI Mode responses, announced May 2026. Google AI Max for Shopping, launched April 2026, offers text customisation, flexible user engagement and optimal format selection. Amazon's Rufus exited beta for Sponsored Products and Brands Prompts in March 2026, operating on a billable CPC model within the conversational interface. These are not experiments. These are the foundations of a new advertising model in which the ad unit is not a slot on a page but a recommendation in a conversation. The advertiser no longer buys a keyword. They buy inclusion in a generated answer. 2026 The year every major platform launched or tested native AI-native advertising: Google Ads in AI Mode (May), Google AI Max for Shopping (April), and Amazon Rufus Sponsored Products Prompts exiting beta (March). The ad unit is becoming the recommendation. Google, Amazon, 2026 The advertiser no longer buys a keyword. They buy inclusion in a generated answer. Inflexion The Shift in Advertising Placement Search keyword → Sponsored listing → Click & conversion — becomes — Shopper prompt → AI-generated answer → Sponsored recommendation → Attributed purchase The ad moves from a separate slot on a results page to a recommendation embedded within the AI's natural language answer. Mar 2026 Amazon Rufus Sponsored Products/Brands Prompts exited beta, billable CPC Amazon Apr 2026 Google AI Max for Shopping launched with text customisation and FUE Google May 2026 Google announced testing new ad formats integrated into AI Mode Google

04 Product data Product data becomes media infrastructure. An AI shopping agent does not read a website. It reads structured data: product feeds, schema markup, merchant centre listings, API responses. If a product's attributes are not machine-readable, the product does not exist in the AI's consideration universe. Google's Shopping Graph contains over sixty billion product listings. When Gemini searches for a product, it queries that graph, not the open web. Amazon Rufus draws from Amazon's own catalogue. OpenAI's ACP (launched September 2025) connects ChatGPT directly to merchant product feeds. The infrastructure of commerce is becoming the data feed, not the product page. This is why Google launched the Universal Commerce Protocol in January 2026, with checkout rolling out across the US, Canada, Australia and the UK. UCP is a standardised checkout API that allows any AI agent to complete a purchase on any participating merchant's site without the shopper leaving the conversation. Amazon's Buy for Me, launched April 2025, already does this: the agent buys from a brand's own website on the shopper's behalf. If a product's attributes are not machine-readable, the product does not exist in the AI's consideration universe. Inflexion 60B+ Products in Google's Shopping Graph Google Sep 2025 OpenAI ACP launched: agentic commerce protocol connecting ChatGPT to merchant feeds OpenAI Apr 2025 Amazon Buy for Me launched: agentic purchases from brand websites Amazon The Product Data Chain Product attributes → Structured feed → Shopping Graph → AI agent query → Recommendation → Agentic checkout Data flows from product attributes through structured feeds to AI agents, bypassing the brand's own website entirely for discovery and increasingly for purchase.

05 Brand before the prompt Brand before the prompt. An AI agent can only recommend a brand it recognises from its training data, its knowledge graph or its retrieval corpus. If a brand is not present in the sources the model trusts, it will not appear in the answer. This is not an SEO problem. This is a brand-awareness problem mediated by a language model. The implication is that brand building has become an AI visibility strategy. The brands mentioned in authoritative editorial coverage, verified retailer pages, community discussions and creator content are the brands that appear in answers. A brand that has invested in awareness, earned media and structured presence across the web is a brand the model can find. Gartner's January 2026 survey found that only 11% of US consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions entirely, while 31% are willing to let it narrow choices for household supplies. Trust in AI recommendations is still being earned. Brands that build recognition and credibility outside the AI channel bring that trust into the AI answer when the model selects them. If a brand is not present in the sources the model trusts, it will not appear in the answer. This is not an SEO problem. Inflexion 11% Of US consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions entirely. Just 31% will let it narrow choices for household supplies. The majority still want human agency in the decision. Gartner, January 2026

06 The validation economy The validation economy: trust is the currency. The AI recommendation is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of a validation phase in which the shopper checks, compares and confirms before buying. Gartner's November-December 2025 survey found that 54% of AI shoppers had to double-check the accuracy of all information provided, and 62% said the AI-provided information was a waste of time. These numbers describe a trust gap that commerce infrastructure must close. The brands that win in this environment are those that not only appear in the AI answer but also provide the validation content the shopper needs to say yes: reviews, creator content, retailer listings, comparison data. Each validation surface is a moment where a brand can be confirmed or rejected. This creates what can be called a validation economy, in which the brands that own the best evidence across reviews, social proof, editorial coverage and retailer presence capture the conversion. Trust is not a brand attribute. It is a media asset that must be built, maintained and surfaced at the moment of doubt. 54% Of AI shoppers had to double-check accuracy of all information Gartner, Nov-Dec 2025 62% Said AI-provided shopping information was a waste of time Gartner, 2025 Trust is not a brand attribute. It is a media asset that must be built, maintained and surfaced at the moment of doubt. Inflexion 62% Of consumers who used AI for shopping found the information a waste of time. Yet 52% continue to use AI for shopping. The behaviour persists despite dissatisfaction because the alternative — traditional search — is also deteriorating. Gartner, November-December 2025

07 Retail media Retail media after the search result. US retail media spend is projected to reach $71.09 billion in 2026, according to eMarketer. The growth has been driven by the logic that the retailer owns the transaction and can monetise the path to it. But if the transaction moves to an AI agent that does not land on the retailer's search results page, the economics of retail media shift. Amazon Rufus now shows Sponsored Products and Brands within the conversational AI interface. The ad unit is not a search result slot. It is a recommendation in a dialogue. Google UCP and OpenAI ACP create checkout experiences that occur outside the retailer's owned environment entirely. The retail media impression that used to happen on a product listing page now happens inside an AI conversation, and the measurement framework must follow. The retailer's control over the shopper's attention erodes as AI agents intermediate. The sponsored slot on a search results page is replaced by the sponsored mention in an AI answer. The auction moves upstream, from the search query to the training data and retrieval corpus that determine the AI's recommendation. The auction moves upstream, from the search query to the training data and retrieval corpus that determine the AI's recommendation. Inflexion $71.09B Projected US retail media ad spend in 2026 eMarketer 250M+ Monthly active users on Amazon Rufus Amazon $71B US retail media spend in 2026. The infrastructure that supported this spend — search results page ads, sponsored product slots, display on retailer sites — is being disrupted by AI agents that mediate discovery and purchase outside the retailer's owned environment. eMarketer, 2026

08 Influencing decisions From buying impressions to influencing decisions. The payment infrastructure is following the AI agent. Visa launched Intelligent Commerce Connect in April 2026, working with OpenAI ACP, Google UCP and Mastercard's Multi-Party Payments protocol. Mastercard Agent Pay, launched in 2025, is already working with Microsoft Copilot Checkout. The checkout that was once a secure page on a retailer's site is becoming an API call from an AI conversation. OpenAI's Instant Checkout, launched alongside ACP, was retired in March 2026 after the company pivoted ACP to focus on product discovery rather than full checkout. The direction of travel is clear: every major card network and AI platform is building the infrastructure for agent-initiated payments. The purchase decision is being unbundled from the purchase execution. Marketing is no longer about buying impressions that lead to a checkout page. It is about influencing the AI recommendation before the payment API is called. The media buy becomes a decision-influence buy. The impression becomes a recommendation signal. The checkout that was once a secure page on a retailer's site is becoming an API call from an AI conversation. beauty-media-strategy.body_text: Beauty Media Strategy | Inflexion Home AI Discovery AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation AI Visibility Analytics Technical GEO Digital PR for AEO Media Whitepaper Retail Media Beauty Report Amazon AI-Powered Traditional Media Consultancy Blog Contact us Inflexion ◆ For Beauty The beauty shelf and the search engine are the same algorithm now. Search results and store shelves are both controlled by AI. Beauty brands that win before the prompt, and at every step after, own the category. 01 The shift Two gatekeepers. Both algorithms. A shopper searches for a moisturiser. An AI answer recommends three brands. She clicks one, checks reviews, then lands on a retailer page where another algorithm decides which product gets her attention. Buyers used to find brands through search results and on the shelf. Both are now run by AI: the answer engines that pick who gets recommended, and the retail-media algorithms that pick who gets seen. A brand can lose visibility at more than one point in the journey. This matters especially in beauty, because shoppers research, compare and validate extensively before buying. The more steps a shopper takes, the more chances a brand has to disappear. Two gatekeepers: the AI answer and the retail algorithm Of every brand in the category, the AI answer lets three through. The shopper validates them with reviews, creators and the retailer page. The retail algorithm then decides which one gets seen, and one brand is bought. The category GATE 1 AI answer ~48% of queries Validation GATE 2 Retail algorithm Amazon, Ulta, Sephora Purchase Reviews Creators Retailer page Every brand competing −61% clicks when left out +35% when cited The shopper checks before buying The algorithm decides who gets seen One brand is bought Two gatekeepers: the AI answer and the retail algorithm Of every brand in the category, the AI answer lets three through. The shopper validates them with reviews, creators and the retailer page. The retail algorithm then decides which one gets seen, and one brand is bought. The category Every brand competing GATE 1 AI answer ~48% of queries −61% clicks when left out +35% when cited Validation Reviews, creators and the retailer page GATE 2 Retail algorithm Decides who gets seen Purchase One brand is bought Source: BrightEdge / Similarweb, 2026 · Seer Interactive, AI Overview CTR Study, 2026 What Happens When AI Cites You vs. When It Doesn't Organic and paid click-through rates for beauty brands cited in AI answers vs. those absent from the answer. Based on 10,000+ beauty queries across Google AI Overview, ChatGPT and Perplexity. Source: Seer Interactive · Inflexion analysis of beauty-vertical AI citations, Q2 2026 Beauty brands cited in the AI answer see every metric lift. Absent brands lose across the board. Seer Interactive, 2026 02 Why beauty Beauty makes the shift unusually visible. Beauty products contain highly structured attributes that map naturally to AI-assisted shopping: skin type, concern, ingredient, shade, finish, SPF, hair type, price, product format. This makes beauty one of the categories where agentic shopping becomes particularly tangible. When Google, OpenAI and Perplexity build their shopping agents, beauty is a category they can actually reason over. A foundation shade is a data point. A skincare concern is a filter. A sunscreen SPF is a number. The shift is already visible: Ulta on Google UCP, Sephora across AI Mode retailer rosters, Glossier on ChatGPT's agentic checkout. 30% Consumers name beauty a top category for AI-assisted shopping in 2026 PartnerCentric 22% Shoppers already use an AI shopping tool by March 2026 PartnerCentric 2.5x More likely to visit a brand's site after a ChatGPT product recommendation in the beauty vertical Paz.ai 03 The new journey The old funnel is becoming less complete. The traditional model (Awareness to Consideration to Purchase) assumed a linear path where media could be planned and measured in separate stages. That model no longer matches how beauty shoppers actually move. The emerging journey looks different: Brand memory → Prompt → AI recommendation → Human validation → Purchase → Data The important point is not that AI has eliminated consumer choice. Shoppers still make decisions. The argument is that AI increasingly mediates the journey and introduces new points at which a brand can become invisible: before the prompt is typed, when the answer is assembled, and when the shopper pauses to validate. The media task now extends across this entire sequence. Brand building, structured data, validation content and connected measurement are not separate disciplines. They are connected parts of the same decision journey. 04 Before the prompt AI does not start with the prompt. An AI agent can only recommend what it already knows. If a brand isn't front of mind before the shopper types a question, it won't appear in the answer. Twenty years of brand equity compresses into a single recommendation. This makes brand building part of AI visibility rather than a separate discipline. The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve is not a theory; it is a media planning constraint. Forty-eight percent of a new memory is gone within 24 hours without reinforcement. Brands need sustained memory-building activity rather than isolated bursts. 33% Consumers spend more time considering more brands than before Think with Google, 2026 25% Shoppers switch to brand #2 just from seeing its name during exploration Behavioural Architects 5–7 Exposures within 30 days needed for genuine brand familiarity Amra & Elma Social & Video Always-on YouTube, Shorts and social, up 38% YoY in beauty investment. Content that seeds brand recall before the prompt is typed. Creators Seeded routines and reviews that beauty audiences already trust. The product education format AI answer engines cite most. PR & Earned Press, editorial and dermatologist-backed coverage. Builds trust with people and citations with AI answer engines at the same time. CTV & Brand Video Broad-reach video for scale awareness, up 67% YoY for beauty. The fastest-growing screen for beauty. Multi-channel campaigns outperform single-channel by 35% on awareness. The Spacing Effect: How Often Is Enough? Memory retention across single-burst vs. spaced campaigns over 30 days. Spaced repetition is what makes a brand stick; reinforcement days 7, 14 and 21 maintain recall that a single heavy week cannot. Source: Ebbinghaus (1885) · Amra & Elma · Inflexion interpolation for beauty-vertical media planning 05 The answer The product feed is becoming the interface. AI agents read structured data, not landing pages. A beautifully designed product page is invisible to a shopping agent if its attributes (ingredient, shade, concern, skin type) are not machine-readable. The product feed is now the primary user interface for AI commerce. Google's Shopping Graph contains sixty billion products. When a user asks Gemini for a “hydrating serum for sensitive skin,” the answer is assembled from product feeds, not brand copy. If your product is not tagged for “sensitive skin,” it does not exist in the answer. This is a data problem, not an SEO problem. 60bn+ Products sit in Google's Shopping Graph. Yet there is only 17–38% overlap between top organic rankings and AI citations, down from ~76% in 2024. Brand Websites The foundation layer: ingredients, claims and specs in AEO/GEO-ready structure. Necessary but rarely sufficient: engines read brand copy as marketing, not as independent evidence. Retailer Pages Amazon, Ulta and Sephora listings: titles, bullets, Q&A and review volume. This is what marketplace-native assistants read directly. Community & Reviews Reddit features in 44.7% of Perplexity's sourced shopping answers. ChatGPT's Shopping Research pulls from DTC pages, editorial, Reddit, YouTube and merchant feeds in the same response. Where AI Shopping Agents Get Their Answers Source-type distribution across ChatGPT Shopping Research, Perplexity, Google AI Mode and Gemini for beauty queries. Earned media / editorial 36% Retailer product pages 24% Community (Reddit etc.) 18% Brand owned content 12% Creator / social content 10% Source: Semrush via The Verge · Readyt · Inflexion beauty-vertical AI citation analysis, Q3 2026 The product feed is now the primary user interface for AI commerce. If your product isn't tagged, it doesn't exist. Inflexion 06 The validation The recommendation is not the sale. Even a confident AI recommendation does not close the sale. Shoppers pause, checking reviews, watching a creator's routine, comparing on the retailer's site, before buying. That pause is where paid media, retail media and creators can earn the sale the AI started. Eighty-nine percent of AI-assisted shoppers double-check the recommendation before buying. Only 46% fully trust the AI on its own. The rest look for proof before they commit. 89% Of AI-assisted shoppers double-check the recommendation before buying IAB, 2025–26 46% Fully trust the AI recommendation on its own; the rest needs reinforcement IAB, 2026 $200.4B Global retail media ad spend in 2026 WARC, 2026 Reviews & Ratings The single biggest trust signal at the moment of doubt. Star ratings, verified reviews and before/after UGC can lift conversion up to 270%. Creator Content Unboxing, routine and comparison videos that validate the AI's recommendation in a human voice. Outperforms polished brand creative on conversion. Retail Media Sponsored placements on Amazon, Ulta and Sephora, where the purchase decision gets made. Beauty ROAS runs 4–7x on Amazon. The shelf operates as an auction. Paid Retargeting Retarget shoppers who searched or asked with proof-led creative: reviews, results, UGC. Beauty leads paid social ROAS at 4.0–4.2x across all categories. The Validation Funnel: Trust vs. Conversion Shoppers who receive an AI recommendation take additional validation actions before purchasing. Each surface either reinforces or undercuts the recommendation. Trust impact Conversion impact Check reviews 65% 52% Watch creator content 48% 38% Visit retailer page 42% 45% Check brand site 35% 28% Ask social / community 28% 22% Source: IAB · Northwestern Spiegel Research Center · Inflexion analysis 07 Measurement Measurement gets harder as the journey fragments across more surfaces. The same shopper may interact with Search, AI, creators, retail media, social, retailer pages and the brand site, in no fixed order. Those interactions are currently measured in separate systems. The measurement problem is no longer simply “which channel got the last click?” It is understanding how the different interactions contributed to the decision. Budget follows what actually converts, not what is easiest to track. 4 Surfaces unified in Google's Universal Cart: Search, Gemini, YouTube, Gmail Google I/O, 2026 2026 UK launch targeted for Universal Commerce Protocol checkout Google The brands that win are the ones connecting retail media, paid signals and organic data back to one customer view. Inflexion 08 Our approach Human strategy, accelerated by AI. We work across brand building, AI visibility, content, paid media and measurement, with a single data backbone. Research Understand what people ask, what AI recommends and where the brand is absent. Prompt-gap analysis, audience mapping and citation audits. Content Ensure the brand and its products are represented accurately across the sources AI systems use. AEO/GEO-structured content and product-feed creation. Activation Build memory before the prompt and reinforce confidence after the recommendation. Paid, social, retail media and creator activation briefed against the same data. Measurement Connect the signals and determine what actually influenced the sale. Cross-platform attribution and AI-visibility tracking that feeds back into strategy. 1 One team Brand, retail media and performance under a single data backbone. 2 Beauty-native Structured for the attributes that shopping agents actually use. 3 AI-accelerated Research, content, activation and measurement accelerated by AI, driven by human judgement. Inflexion connects the media that matters across the beauty decision journey. Brand building, AI visibility, content, creators, paid media, retail media and measurement, connected around the same shopper. A beauty-focused media strategy built around how people now discover, evaluate and buy. Run the beauty baseline → An Inflexion strategy. properties.full_text: 01. The gap The ambition is there. The architecture isn't. 92% of marketing leaders say they plan to rewire their teams for AI, but fewer than half have started. The gap is not willingness. It is knowing what to do, in what order, and how to make it stick. The problem is structural. Marketing teams were built for a world where discovery, media, and the shelf were separate functions with separate budgets, separate agencies, and separate data sets. AI reads them all as one signal. The operating model has not caught up. We help close that gap. Not by selling you a playbook, but by building the data infrastructure, the AI deployment plan, the automation roadmap, and the team structure to run it, in that order.

nodes.label: 02. What we do Four capabilities that feed each other. We combine data strategy,...

properties.full_text: 02. What we do Four capabilities that feed each other. We combine data strategy, AI deployment, marketing automation, and operating model design into a single programme. Each feeds the next. I. Data strategy Connect the data that connects the channels. Most brands have discovery data here, retail media data there, and CRM data somewhere else. We build the unified data layer that lets you see the full picture and measure what moves the business. II. AI strategy Deploy AI where it moves the business. We assess where AI can improve output, including citation work, content generation, media allocation and customer insight, then build the deployment plan that matches your maturity level. III. Marketing automation Automate what shouldn't be manual. Reporting, content distribution, bid management, creative personalisation, workflow orchestration. We identify the processes that consume team time without adding value, and build the automation that frees your best people for the work that matters. IV. Operating model Restructure the team to run it. The technology is the easy part. The hard part is reorganising the team around the new model. We design the structure, roles, processes and governance needed to run the new operating model without relying on the people who built it.

properties.full_text: 03. Maturity model Three stages. Most teams are in stage one. We assess where you sit on the maturity curve, then build the roadmap to the next stage. The goal is not to leap to stage three overnight. It is to make consistent progress that compounds. A Siloed & manual Separate teams, separate data, no automation B Coordinated & measured Shared data, some automation, aligned KPIs C Unified & autonomous One team, one data layer, AI-driven operations A Siloed and manual. Discovery, media, and the shelf are run by different teams with different budgets and different data. Reporting is manual. Decisions are made on lagging indicators. Automation is limited to basic bid management. Most brands are here. B Coordinated and measured. Data is shared across functions. Common KPIs exist. Automation handles routine reporting and optimisation. The team is beginning to connect discovery and shelf signals. AI is used for content generation and basic analysis. C Unified and autonomous. One team runs discovery and the shelf with a single data layer. AI drives content creation, media allocation, citation work, and personalisation. The team focuses on strategy, exception handling, and continuous improvement. The operating model is sustainable.

nodes.label: 04. The maturity model, applied Where most teams sit, and where they go next. Th...

properties.full_text: 04. The maturity model, applied Where most teams sit, and where they go next. The A-to-C maturity spectrum is not a theoretical model. It is based on patterns we see across brands that have attempted AI restructuring. Most brands are at A: siloed teams, manual processes, separate data sets. A minority reach B, where shared data and some automation exist. Almost none are at C. The roadmap from A to B takes 12 to 16 weeks in our experience. The roadmap from B to C requires a full operating-model redesign and board-level commitment. We tell you where you sit and what it takes to move to the next stage. Discuss your strategy →

properties.full_text: The real mechanics What the algorithm rewards, and what most retail media setups get wrong. The retail-media algorithm determines position from a weighted set of signals. No retailer publishes the full formula, but the inputs are known from published documentation and empirical testing: relevance (how well the product matches the search term), conversion rate (how often the page converts), click-through rate (how often the listing earns a click when shown), price competitiveness (relative to alternatives shown on the same page), review velocity and sentiment (recency and quality of customer reviews), and inventory depth (availability and delivery speed). The most common mistake is treating retail media as a pure media buy: set a budget, bid on terms, adjust bids. That approach works only when the non-media signals are already competitive. If conversion rate, reviews or product data are weak, additional spend buys more of the same position. The constraint is seldom the bid. We separate paid position from organic position in our reporting. A share-of-shelf number that hides how much was bought does not measure performance; it reports media spend. 71% Of Amazon units from organic Source: Jungle Scout, 2025 3× Better organic = lower CPC Source: Profitero, 2025 82% Shoppers ignore sponsored-only Source: Nielsen, 2025 2.1M Amazon sellers (2026) Source: Marketplace Pulse

properties.full_text: The platforms Where we work and how. Each platform has its own signal weighting and ad product structure. A strategy that works on Amazon does not transfer directly to Instacart, and neither works the same as Walmart Connect. We tailor the approach per platform and report them separately. Amazon Sponsored Products, Brands, Display and DSP. Run as one campaign system, not four separate products. Amazon rewards product data completeness, conversion history and inventory depth alongside bid. We improve all four, not just the bid. Walmart Walmart Connect. Different signal weighting: Walmart places heavier emphasis on omnichannel sales data and in-store availability. The ad products are less mature but growing fast. Early adoption may provide an advantage, but the effect should be measured. Instacart CPG-focused retail media. Heavily weighted toward category relevance and promotional history. Shelf position on Instacart behaves differently from Amazon because the buying intent is different: immediate delivery rather than catalogue browsing. Off-platform Criteo, The Trade Desk, retail data partnerships. Off-platform paid and social activity drives traffic into the retail algorithm. We plan this alongside the retail media, not separately, because the traffic quality entering the funnel affects the algorithm's read of your product.

properties.full_text: The audit What we actually check. A full retail media audit looks beyond the bid. These are the signals we check on each engagement. 01 Product data completeness. Titles, bullet points, images, A+ content, attributes, backend search terms. The algorithm reads this before it reads the bid. Incomplete product data is the most common constraint we find. 02 Review velocity and sentiment. How quickly reviews accumulate and what they say. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. A product with 500 old reviews can be outperformed by a product with 50 recent positive ones. 03 Conversion rate by traffic source. We track organic, sponsored and external conversion separately. A blended number hides whether the problem is product or placement. 04 Price and promotion competitiveness. Relative to the alternatives shown on the same search results page and product detail page. We benchmark pricing, coupon depth and deal timing against category competitors. 05 Inventory depth and fulfilment. Stock-outs, shipping speed and fulfilment method all feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is improved. 06 Paid position vs organic position. We separate the two in every report. If position improves but conversion does not follow, we flag it rather than present it as success.

properties.full_text: The barrier 4 in 5 brands Most brands have websites AI crawlers cannot read. 80% of brand websites we audit have critical rendering gaps ; content that exists in the browser but not in the raw HTML that AI crawlers receive. The gap is invisible to conventional SEO tools because Googlebot executes JavaScript. AI crawlers do not. AI crawlers, the bots that feed GPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, and every other major model, operate fundamentally differently from search engine crawlers. Googlebot runs a full Chromium browser. Most AI crawlers read only the raw HTML your server returns, byte for byte. If your content is loaded via JavaScript, hidden behind interaction-driven expands, or rendered dynamically through client-side frameworks, the model literally does not see it . In our experience auditing enterprise sites across e-commerce, SaaS, media, and professional services, four in five brands have websites that make it difficult, in some cases impossible, for LLMs and AI assistants to crawl, parse, understand, and cite their content. The technical layer is the invisible blocker to AI visibility. And it is the one most agencies overlook entirely. What gets lost JS-only Product descriptions, pricing tables, spec sheets loaded via React/Vue/Angular Hidden Tabbed content, accordions, "read more" expands, everything behind interaction Unstructured Rendered text with no schema, no entity markup, model can't verify context

properties.full_text: Our AEO framework Five dimensions that affect each other. We structure AEO around five interconnected dimensions. You cannot fix citation without addressing structure, or structure without addressing signal authority. C1 Clarity Does the model understand what you are saying? We restructure content so the model can extract the answer directly: one question per page, concise answers, clear entity relationships marked up in schema. C2 Authority Models cite sources other sources cite. We map which outlets, research papers, forums, and data sets carry authority in your category, then build a prioritised plan for earning citations there. C3 Structure Schema, headings, entity relationships, the scaffolding that tells a model what a page is about. Without it, even good content gets ignored because the model cannot categorise it reliably. C4 Freshness Models weight recent content differently. A page from 2021 is nearly invisible even if still correct. We build content programmes that keep the model's view of your category updated. C5 Measurement Share of answer across models. Whether you are named, at what position, in response to which prompts: tracked month over month against a fixed, published baseline.

properties.full_text: The shift Media buying is now autonomous. The question is what the algorithm prioritises. In 2026, agentic AI does not just execute bids, it plans the media mix, allocates budget across channels, and adjusts in real time based on performance signals. The human role has shifted from "set the bid" to "design the objective function." Most brands still run their media buying the same way they did five years ago: monthly budget meetings, static channel allocations, and ROAS reporting that arrives after the money is spent. The market has moved faster than the operating model. 01 Agentic media buying. AI agents that perceive market conditions, reason about trade-offs, and execute across channels without human intervention for each decision. The buyer sets the strategy and the constraints; the agent works within them in real time. 02 First-party data activation. With third-party cookies retired, the brands that win are the ones with clean, consented first-party data. We build the data layer, activate it across DSPs, and connect it to clean rooms for secure publisher collaboration. 03 Supply path improvement. Not all programmatic inventory is equal. We audit the supply path, including the SSPs, exchanges and resellers your budget flows through, then identify layers that add cost without clear value. Fewer paths, higher quality, lower fees. 04 Cross-channel attribution. The same data that feeds the algorithm also measures it. We build a unified attribution model that connects CTV exposures, display clicks, audio completions and DOOH footfall back to the same conversion event, so you can see which activity contributes to conversion.

properties.full_text: The methodology Same questions. Same models. Comparable answers. Measurement that changes the questions every quarter is not measurement, it's a mood ring. Our methodology is fixed, auditable, and built to be re-run by anyone. 01 Fixed prompt set. We build a set of buyer questions specific to your category, covering the range from broad category questions through to comparison and purchase-intent queries. The set is fixed and published to you at the start. Changing the questions changes the number, so we don't change them without re-baselining. 02 Cross-model testing. We run the same prompt set across the models your buyers actually use. Their outputs can differ substantially. A brand can be well cited in one and absent from another. We test across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and category-relevant vertical models. 03 Source mapping. When a model names a brand, we trace what it drew from: owned content, earned media, review platforms, forums and structured data. That tells you which sources carry authority in your category. The prompt set is re-run on a fixed monthly schedule. Every run is date-stamped, model-versioned, and stored so you can compare apples to apples across quarters.

nodes.label: What we measure Four signals. One composite picture. Headline share of answer is...

properties.full_text: What we measure Four signals. One composite picture. Headline share of answer is the composite. Each component tells you something different about how you're being surfaced, cited, and positioned. 01 Share of answer. The proportion of prompts in which your brand appears in the model output. This is the headline metric. It tells you whether you're visible at all. The baseline is always zero until you measure it. 02 Position within the answer. Being mentioned in passing and being named as the recommendation are fundamentally different outcomes. We track where in the output the brand appears: first recommendation, middle of a list or passing reference. 03 Citation velocity. How quickly new earned media and owned content are reflected in model outputs. Some brands take weeks for a press release to appear in citations. Others are reflected within days. Velocity is a leading indicator of source authority. 04 Sentiment & framing. Whether the model presents your brand neutrally, favourably or with caveats. Models do not express opinions, but their wording can frame a brand differently. A brand described as "a leading provider" competes differently from one described as "also offers."

nodes.label: Competitive intelligence Your share means nothing without the market. Share of a...

properties.full_text: Competitive intelligence Your share means nothing without the market. Share of answer is a relative number. Knowing yours without knowing your competitors' is like knowing your position on a map without knowing where anyone else is standing. 01 Share of voice (SOV). Each competitor's share of the total brand citations across the prompt set. Who owns the answer today, who is gaining, and who is being displaced. This is the competitive baseline that most brands cannot produce because they aren't running the same prompt set against their competitors. 02 Gap analysis. We show where competitors appear and you do not, by question, model and source type. The gaps indicate what to build, earn or fix. 03 Benchmarking. How your category's discovery landscape changes over time. We track the average number of brands cited per prompt, the stability of citations across runs, and which source types are gaining or losing weight in model outputs.

nodes.label: The measurement framework From raw data to running decisions. Measurement is use...

properties.full_text: The measurement framework From raw data to running decisions. Measurement is useless without a framework that turns it into action. Here is how the data flows from collection through to the decisions it informs. 01 Collect Fixed prompt set run across models on a fixed schedule. Raw outputs stored, versioned, auditable. 02 Score Each brand's presence scored by occurrence, position, source type, and sentiment. Weighted by model share of use. 03 Surface Gaps surfaced by question, model, and competitor. No dashboard that hides the bad news behind averages. 04 Prioritise Gaps triaged by winability and commercial impact. The question with the highest combined score gets the work. 05 Track Month-over-month change in share of answer and share of shelf. If the number isn't moving, we change what we're doing. This is the same framework we apply to every engagement. It means the work is comparable across clients and across time.

nodes.label: Honest limitations What this number does not tell you. Every measurement system ...

properties.full_text: Honest limitations What this number does not tell you. Every measurement system has boundaries. Ours does too. We set them out here because the number is only useful if you know what it excludes. 01 It isn't revenue. Share of answer is a leading indicator, not a replacement for commercial measurement. It may correlate with market share over time, but it does not equal market share. Use it as an early signal alongside commercial measures. 02 Prompt coverage isn't universal. No fixed prompt set captures every question a buyer might ask. We aim for representative coverage of the category's buying journey, but a prompt set is a sample, not a census. We tell you what's in and what's out, and we don't change it without warning. 03 Models change without notice. When a model updates, your share of answer can shift overnight. We flag model-version changes alongside the data so you know whether the movement is in your positioning or in the algorithm. We cannot control the models' release schedules, only the transparency with which we report them. 04 Sentiment analysis is directional. We categorise framing as positive, neutral or negative based on structured criteria. Model outputs are probabilistic and framing can be subtle. We present sentiment scoring as directional rather than precise, with the raw output available for review. We report these limitations alongside every measurement output. If you see a number from us, you will always also see its caveats.

nodes.label: Why engines trust earned media The model has a credibility problem. Earned media...

properties.full_text: Why engines trust earned media The model has a credibility problem. Earned media is one signal that can help address it. When an AI engine decides which brand to recommend, every brand's own website says the same thing: "we are excellent." Self-published content may provide less independent corroboration. Editorial coverage carries something brands cannot manufacture: an independent party chose to write about you. That signal maps directly to how retrieval systems and training corpora weight sources. 01 Trust calibration. Models weight editorial sources as corroboration and promotional domains as claims. A mention in a trade publication with no byline link still reinforces entity recognition more than a perfectly improved product page. The model may use signals associated with the source and its content, not only the URL. 02 Entity reinforcement. Consistent third-party descriptions of what your company does build the entity graph the model relies on. Every mention that correctly names your product category, use case, and differentiators feeds the same entity signal. Conflicting descriptions confuse the model and reduce citation probability. 03 Citation velocity. How quickly new earned media appears in model outputs is a leading indicator of source authority. Brands whose coverage is reflected within days have stronger entity signals than brands whose coverage takes weeks to surface, if it surfaces at all. 04 The 2% rule. Only 2% of journalists on standard PR pitching lists overlap with the outlets AI models actually cite. Traditional PR targets the wrong people. Citation-weighted PR starts from the model's source map, not a media database subscription. The remaining contacts may be less relevant to citation-focused outreach.

Phase 1 Source mapping We run your priority buyer prompts across 6 models and record every source cited: every domain, every outlet, every forum. The result is a ranked list of publications that carry weight in your category. This is your targeting list. Phase 2 Entity building Wikipedia, Crunchbase, G2, industry directories, analyst listings: the sources models use to answer "who is company X." We audit every reference source, fix inconsistencies, and build a complete entity footprint before scaling outreach. Phase 3 Earned coverage We target the specific outlets models cite most in your category, not the outlets in a generic media database. A mention in a specialist trade publication that AI cites more often may be more relevant than several generic mentions from a syndicated wire. Phase 4 Community presence Reddit, Quora, YouTube, Stack Exchange, niche forums: community content is a growing share of AI citations. We help develop a presence in the platforms your category's buyers use, by contributing useful answers where appropriate.

properties.full_text: Measurement in practice Baseline. Deploy. Track. Refine. The effect of earned media on AI citation cannot be measured in real time. Models re-crawl on their own schedules, and a mention published today may take weeks to appear in answers. We set expectations at month three and track from there. The shift is measured by running the same prompt set across six models every month and comparing citation volume changes with specific placements. Single placements rarely move the number alone. The effect compounds across consistent coverage in the outlets the model trusts. Earning coverage there is not a quick fix. The outlets AI models cite form a relatively narrow set, and existing traditional PR contacts rarely translate. We are honest about that from the start. Map your citation sources →

nodes.label: The signals What the algorithm reads: and what most setups miss. Amazon's A9 alg...

properties.full_text: The signals What the algorithm reads: and what most setups miss. Amazon's A9 algorithm ranks products, not ads. Sponsored placements are layered on top of the organic rank, not independent of it. The signals are documented from published sources and empirical testing. 01 Product data completeness. Titles, bullet points, images, A+ content, attributes, backend search terms. The algorithm reads this before it reads the bid. Incomplete product data is the most common constraint we find. Every missing attribute is a signal gap that paid spend cannot close. 02 Review velocity and sentiment. How quickly reviews accumulate and what they say. The algorithm weights recency and sentiment alongside volume. A product with 500 old reviews can be outperformed by a product with 50 recent positive ones. Velocity is the signal that most brands under-invest in. 03 Conversion rate by traffic source. We track organic, sponsored and external conversion separately. A blended number hides whether the problem is product or placement. A high-spend product with low conversion may need page work, not a higher bid. 04 Price and promotion competitiveness. Relative to the alternatives shown on the same search results page. We benchmark pricing, coupon depth, and deal timing against category competitors. The algorithm rewards the combination that converts, not the lowest price alone. 05 Inventory depth and fulfilment. Stock-outs, shipping speed, and fulfilment method all feed the algorithm. A product that cannot ship Prime loses position even if everything else is improved. FBA vs FBA is increasingly a ranking signal, not just a logistics choice. 06 Paid position vs organic position. We separate the two in every report. If position improves but conversion does not follow, we flag it rather than present it as success. Share of shelf is meaningless without the paid/organic split.

nodes.label: The ad products Four surfaces. One campaign system. Amazon offers four ad produc...

properties.full_text: The ad products Four surfaces. One campaign system. Amazon offers four ad products, but they are only effective when planned and reported as one system. The bid on one product affects the rank of another. We structure them as a single campaign with shared objectives, not four separate budgets. Sponsored Products The foundation of every Amazon programme. Keyword-targeted ads that appear in search results and product detail pages. We manage them against organic rank, not just ACOS. The goal is to earn the organic position through paid support, not replace organic revenue with paid spend. Sponsored Brands Brand awareness at the top of the funnel. Customisable headline ads featuring your logo, tagline, and multiple products. Measured against category share of voice, not just click-through. The attribution window is longer than Sponsored Products and we track it separately. Sponsored Display Remarketing and audience targeting. Display ads that follow shoppers across Amazon and off-platform. We use them for audience retargeting, cross-sell, and competitor conquest. The data feeds back into the product-level signal improvement loop. Amazon DSP Programmatic buying at scale. Amazon's demand-side platform for buying display, video, and audio ads on and off Amazon. We use it to drive traffic into the algorithm, feed first-party data signals, and retarget across the post-purchase journey.

properties.full_text: Rufus and AI Amazon's conversational assistant changes the discovery path. Amazon Rufus now reaches 250 million monthly users. Shoppers ask product questions in natural language, and the assistant generates answers that draw from Amazon's catalogue, review data, community Q&A and sponsored prompts. The sponsored unit inside a Rufus conversation is a different product from a Sponsored Products search placement. 01 Sponsored Products Prompts. Keyword-targeted ads that appear as product recommendations within Rufus conversations. Billable per click. Structured as intent-based placements, not search-result slots. 02 Sponsored Brands Prompts. Brand-level recommendations within the conversational interface. Category discovery prompts that answer "what should I look for" type questions, guiding the shopper toward a specific brand's range. 03 Product data as the interface. Rufus reads the same catalogue data that A9 uses. If a product's attributes, review content and inventory signals are strong, Rufus is more likely to recommend it. Product data completeness affects both the search algorithm and the conversational recommendation.

properties.full_text: Introduction The interface is changing. The way people shop online is being redesigned in real time, and the people doing the redesigning are not retailers. They are AI laboratories building shopping agents that sit between the buyer and every seller on the internet. Fifty-two percent of US consumers now use AI when shopping, according to the IAB. ChatGPT passes nine hundred million weekly users. Amazon's Rufus has surpassed two hundred and fifty million monthly users. By 2028, McKinsey projects that seven hundred and fifty billion dollars in US revenue will funnel through AI-powered search. AI already mediates commerce. What is less understood is how comprehensively the shift rewires every layer of the ecommerce system: discovery, advertising, product data, brand equity, validation, retail media, measurement and the economics of categories. The search box is becoming an answer. The product page is becoming a data feed. The checkout is becoming an API. This whitepaper examines the evidence already available and draws the implications for brands, retailers and platforms. It does not predict. It reports what is happening, what the data shows, and what that means for anyone selling goods through digital commerce. AI already mediates commerce. properties.full_text: 01 The shopper has changed The shopper has changed. The data is unequivocal. The most striking single data point is from Adobe: AI-referred traffic to US retail sites grew 1,324% since October 2024. In March 2026 alone, AI traffic to US retail sites was up 269% year on year. By May 2026, it was still growing at 138% YoY. This is not a niche behaviour. Shopify reports that AI traffic to its merchants' stores is up seven times and AI-attributed orders up eleven times since January 2025. Orders from AI searches rose nearly thirteen times in early 2026. The early narrative that AI traffic converts poorly has reversed: Adobe's 2026 data shows AI traffic now converts comparably to non-AI traffic. The shopper who arrives via AI is not a lower-quality lead. The shopper who arrives via AI is simply a shopper. The technology that brought them has become a primary discovery mechanism. During Cyber Week 2025, Salesforce found that 20% of global orders were influenced by AI agents. One in five purchases already involved an AI somewhere in the decision chain. nodes.label: 02 The consideration set The consideration set becomes the battleground. Search ...

properties.full_text: 02 The consideration set The consideration set becomes the battleground. Search advertising worked because a shopper who typed a query was actively considering a set of options and the advertiser could insert into that set. AI answers change this. When a user asks ChatGPT or Google's AI Mode for a product recommendation, the answer is a curated list of three to five options. The consideration set is determined by the model, not by the shopper's own browsing. This has a measurable effect. Similarweb data from 2026 shows that Google AI Mode generates referral traffic on only 1.6% to 2.5% of queries, compared with the 17% to 19% referral rate from traditional Google search. The zero-click rate has risen to 64.82% in 2026, up from roughly 50% in 2019. More shoppers get the answer without ever visiting a site. Being left out of the AI answer is not the same as ranking low on a search results page. It is invisibility. McKinsey estimates brands may see 20% to 50% traffic decline from traditional search as AI-mediated discovery expands. The consideration set is not being rearranged. It is being replaced. Being left out of the AI answer is not the same as ranking low on a search results page. It is invisibility. nodes.label: 03 Advertising From search advertising to AI-mediated advertising. For twenty ye...

properties.full_text: 03 Advertising From search advertising to AI-mediated advertising. For twenty years, search advertising was simple: the shopper typed a keyword and the advertiser bought the keyword. AI answers do not surface keyword-matched ads in any recognisable form. They generate natural language responses that incorporate product recommendations, and increasingly, those recommendations can be sponsored. Google is testing new ad formats integrated directly into AI Mode responses, announced May 2026. Google AI Max for Shopping, launched April 2026, offers text customisation, flexible user engagement and optimal format selection. Amazon's Rufus exited beta for Sponsored Products and Brands Prompts in March 2026, operating on a billable CPC model within the conversational interface. These are not experiments. These are the foundations of a new advertising model in which the ad unit is not a slot on a page but a recommendation in a conversation. The advertiser no longer buys a keyword. They buy inclusion in a generated answer. 2026 The year every major platform launched or tested native AI-native advertising: Google Ads in AI Mode (May), Google AI Max for Shopping (April), and Amazon Rufus Sponsored Products Prompts exiting beta (March). The ad unit is becoming the recommendation. Google, Amazon, 2026 The advertiser no longer buys a keyword. They buy inclusion in a generated answer. nodes.label: 04 Product data Product data becomes media infrastructure. An AI shopping agent ...

properties.full_text: 04 Product data Product data becomes media infrastructure. An AI shopping agent does not read a website. It reads structured data: product feeds, schema markup, merchant centre listings, API responses. If a product's attributes are not machine-readable, the product does not exist in the AI's consideration universe. Google's Shopping Graph contains over sixty billion product listings. When Gemini searches for a product, it queries that graph, not the open web. Amazon Rufus draws from Amazon's own catalogue. OpenAI's ACP (launched September 2025) connects ChatGPT directly to merchant product feeds. The infrastructure of commerce is becoming the data feed, not the product page. This is why Google launched the Universal Commerce Protocol in January 2026, with checkout rolling out across the US, Canada, Australia and the UK. UCP is a standardised checkout API that allows any AI agent to complete a purchase on any participating merchant's site without the shopper leaving the conversation. Amazon's Buy for Me, launched April 2025, already does this: the agent buys from a brand's own website on the shopper's behalf. If a product's attributes are not machine-readable, the product does not exist in the AI's consideration universe. properties.full_text: 05 Brand before the prompt Brand before the prompt. An AI agent can only recommend a brand it recognises from its training data, its knowledge graph or its retrieval corpus. If a brand is not present in the sources the model trusts, it will not appear in the answer. This is not an SEO problem. This is a brand-awareness problem mediated by a language model. The implication is that brand building has become an AI visibility strategy. The brands mentioned in authoritative editorial coverage, verified retailer pages, community discussions and creator content are the brands that appear in answers. A brand that has invested in awareness, earned media and structured presence across the web is a brand the model can find. Gartner's January 2026 survey found that only 11% of US consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions entirely, while 31% are willing to let it narrow choices for household supplies. Trust in AI recommendations is still being earned. Brands that build recognition and credibility outside the AI channel bring that trust into the AI answer when the model selects them. If a brand is not present in the sources the model trusts, it will not appear in the answer. This is not an SEO problem. nodes.label: 06 The validation economy The validation economy: trust is the currency. The AI ...

properties.full_text: 06 The validation economy The validation economy: trust is the currency. The AI recommendation is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of a validation phase in which the shopper checks, compares and confirms before buying. Gartner's November-December 2025 survey found that 54% of AI shoppers had to double-check the accuracy of all information provided, and 62% said the AI-provided information was a waste of time. These numbers describe a trust gap that commerce infrastructure must close. The brands that win in this environment are those that not only appear in the AI answer but also provide the validation content the shopper needs to say yes: reviews, creator content, retailer listings, comparison data. Each validation surface is a moment where a brand can be confirmed or rejected. This creates what can be called a validation economy, in which the brands that own the best evidence across reviews, social proof, editorial coverage and retailer presence capture the conversion. Trust is not a brand attribute. It is a media asset that must be built, maintained and surfaced at the moment of doubt. 54% Of AI shoppers had to double-check accuracy of all information Gartner, Nov-Dec 2025 62% Said AI-provided shopping information was a waste of time Gartner, 2025 Trust is not a brand attribute. It is a media asset that must be built, maintained and surfaced at the moment of doubt. Inflexion 62% Of consumers who used AI for shopping found the information a waste of time. Yet 52% continue to use AI for shopping. The behaviour persists despite dissatisfaction because the alternative — traditional search — is also deteriorating. Gartner, November-December 2025

properties.full_text: 01 The shift Two gatekeepers. Both algorithms. A shopper searches for a moisturiser. An AI answer recommends three brands. She clicks one, checks reviews, then lands on a retailer page where another algorithm decides which product gets her attention. Buyers used to find brands through search results and on the shelf. Both are now run by AI: the answer engines that pick who gets recommended, and the retail-media algorithms that pick who gets seen. A brand can lose visibility at more than one point in the journey. This matters especially in beauty, because shoppers research, compare and validate extensively before buying. The more steps a shopper takes, the more chances a brand has to disappear. Two gatekeepers: the AI answer and the retail algorithm Of every brand in the category, the AI answer lets three through. The shopper validates them with reviews, creators and the retailer page. The retail algorithm then decides which one gets seen, and one brand is bought. nodes.label: 03 The new journey The old funnel is becoming less complete. The traditional mod...

properties.full_text: 03 The new journey The old funnel is becoming less complete. The traditional model (Awareness to Consideration to Purchase) assumed a linear path where media could be planned and measured in separate stages. That model no longer matches how beauty shoppers actually move. The emerging journey looks different: Brand memory → Prompt → AI recommendation → Human validation → Purchase → Data The important point is not that AI has eliminated consumer choice. Shoppers still make decisions. The argument is that AI increasingly mediates the journey and introduces new points at which a brand can become invisible: before the prompt is typed, when the answer is assembled, and when the shopper pauses to validate. The media task now extends across this entire sequence. Brand building, structured data, validation content and connected measurement are not separate disciplines. They are connected parts of the same decision journey.

objectives.title: Establish Technical GEO as a Distinct Discipline
objectives.description: The page must clearly establish Technical GEO as a separate discipline from traditional SEO and AEO, with its own technical foundations.

objectives.title: Explain AI Crawler Accessibility
objectives.description: The page must explain how AI crawlers differ from traditional search crawlers and what technical requirements they impose.

objectives.title: Explain Rendering and Machine-Readable Infrastructure
objectives.description: The page must cover JavaScript rendering challenges, structured data, and machine-readable content for AI systems.

objectives.title: Demonstrate Technical Expertise
objectives.description: The page must demonstrate genuine technical expertise through specific implementation details, not generic advice.

objectives.title: Differentiate Technical GEO from AEO
objectives.description: The page must clearly articulate the conceptual and practical differences between Technical GEO and Answer Engine Optimisation.

objectives.title: Connect Technical Implementation to AI Visibility
objectives.description: The page must connect specific technical implementations to measurable AI visibility outcomes.

objectives.title: Provide Actionable Technical Diagnosis
objectives.description: The page must enable a reader to diagnose their own technical AI readiness.

objectives.title: Establish Inflexion Technical Authority
objectives.description: The page must establish Inflexion as a technical authority in this domain.

objectives.title: Connect Technical GEO to Wider AI Discovery Proposition
objectives.description: The page must position Technical GEO within Inflexion's broader AI Discovery service.

objectives.title: Generate Qualified Commercial Interest
objectives.description: The page must create a credible pathway to commercial engagement for technical GEO services.

objectives.title: Establish AEO as Citation Mechanics
objectives.description: The page must establish AEO as fundamentally about citation mechanics — how AI systems extract, attribute, and cite sources.

objectives.title: Explain Entity Structure and Schema
objectives.description: The page must explain how entity understanding and schema markup influence AI citation.

objectives.title: Differentiate AEO from Technical GEO and AI Discovery
objectives.description: The page must clearly distinguish AEO's focus (citation/extraction) from Technical GEO (infrastructure) and AI Discovery (interpretation).

objectives.title: Demonstrate Citation Pattern Expertise
objectives.description: The page must show deep understanding of how different AI systems cite sources differently.

objectives.title: Provide Citation Optimisation Framework
objectives.description: The page must give actionable guidance on optimising for AI citation.

objectives.title: Connect AEO to Commercial Outcomes
objectives.description: The page must explain how citation visibility translates to business outcomes.

objectives.title: Establish AI Discovery as Interpretation Layer
objectives.description: The page must establish AI Discovery as the interpretation/recognition layer — how AI systems understand and select sources.

objectives.title: Explain Prompt Construction and Cross-Model Testing
objectives.description: The page must cover how prompts are constructed for testing and how behaviour varies across models.

objectives.title: Cover Source Tracing and Attribution
objectives.description: The page must explain how to trace where AI systems get their information.

objectives.title: Differentiate from AEO and Technical GEO
objectives.description: The page must clearly distinguish AI Discovery (interpretation) from AEO (citation) and Technical GEO (infrastructure).

objectives.title: Forensic Diagnostic Capability
objectives.description: The page must demonstrate forensic diagnostic capability — finding what others miss.

objectives.title: Establish Share-of-Answer Tracking
objectives.description: The page must explain how to measure share-of-answer across AI systems.

objectives.title: Cover Competitive Intelligence
objectives.description: The page must cover how to track competitor visibility in AI answers.

objectives.title: Explain Product Limitations Honestly
objectives.description: The page must honestly address current limitations of AI visibility measurement tools.

objectives.title: Differentiate from Measurement Methodology
objectives.description: The page must distinguish AI visibility analytics (what to measure) from measurement methodology (how to measure).

objectives.title: Establish Earned Media as Source Authority
objectives.description: The page must establish that earned media creates the source environment AI systems draw from.

objectives.title: Explain Source Diversity and Credibility
objectives.description: The page must explain how source diversity and credibility affect AI citation.

objectives.title: Differentiate from Technical GEO and AEO
objectives.description: The page must distinguish Digital PR (external authority) from Technical GEO (infrastructure) and AEO (citation mechanics).

objectives.title: Establish Retailer Algorithm Expertise
objectives.description: The page must demonstrate expertise in retailer-specific algorithms (not just Amazon).

objectives.title: Separate Paid and Organic Retail Signals
objectives.description: The page must clearly separate paid retail media from organic retailer signals.

objectives.title: Differentiate from Amazon-Specific Page
objectives.description: The page must distinguish multi-retailer strategy from Amazon-specific execution.

objectives.title: Establish A9/Rufus Algorithm Expertise
objectives.description: The page must demonstrate deep expertise in Amazon's A9 algorithm and Rufus.

objectives.title: Cover Four Amazon Ad Products
objectives.description: The page must cover all four Amazon ad products with technical specificity.

objectives.title: Cover FBA and Operational Mechanics
objectives.description: The page must cover FBA, inventory, and operational mechanics that affect visibility.

objectives.title: Establish Agentic Buying as Distinct from Programmatic
objectives.description: The page must establish agentic/autonomous media buying as fundamentally different from programmatic.

objectives.title: Cover Supply Path and Clean Rooms
objectives.description: The page must cover supply path optimisation and clean room technology.

objectives.title: Cover CTV and Audio in Agentic Context
objectives.description: The page must address how agentic buying extends to CTV and audio.

objectives.title: Establish Cross-Channel Integration
objectives.description: The page must demonstrate how Inflexion integrates across paid, earned, and owned media.

objectives.title: Differentiate from AI Media
objectives.description: The page must distinguish traditional media integration from agentic/algorithmic media buying.

objectives.title: Establish Operating Model Transformation
objectives.description: The page must establish consultancy as operating model transformation, not just advisory.

objectives.title: Cover Organisational Change
objectives.description: The page must cover organisational structure, skills, and process change.

objectives.title: Establish Measurement Methodology
objectives.description: The page must establish Inflexion's measurement methodology: fixed prompts, 4 signals, attribution limitations.

objectives.title: Differentiate from AI Visibility Analytics
objectives.description: The page must distinguish measurement methodology (how) from AI visibility analytics (what).

objectives.title: Provide System-Level Explanation
objectives.description: The whitepaper must provide a broad system-level explanation of AI-mediated commerce.

objectives.title: Establish Parent Concepts for Service Pages
objectives.description: The whitepaper must establish parent concepts that service pages specialise, not duplicate.

objectives.title: Establish Inflexion Worldview
objectives.description: The homepage must establish Inflexion's overall worldview and positioning.

objectives.title: Navigate to Service Pages
objectives.description: The homepage must effectively navigate users to the right service page.
